code
# ---- MORE EFFICIENT -----------------------------------
# marginaleffects::slopes() computes this marginal effect AND its delta-method
# SE from the model object, with no hand-written covariance formula:
#
#   library(marginaleffects)
#   slopes(m1, variables = "p1", newdata = datagrid(p1 = seq(0, 20, 2)))
#
# WHY it's better: you never transcribe the "b1 + 2*b2*x" derivative or the
# variance formula, so there's nothing to get wrong -- marginaleffects
# differentiates the prediction numerically and pulls the covariances from V
# itself. The by-hand version is here so the covariance term is visible: that
# middle 4*p*Cov(b1,b2) piece is exactly what a naive SE(b1) + SE(2*b2*x) would
# miss.


Look at the output. The marginal effect of Polity hovers around zero and its interval covers zero everywhere, because neither Polity term is doing anything in this model. That is the point, not a defect: the procedure for the standard error of a linear combination is identical whether or not the effect is real — we compute it the same way for a null result and a strong one. And notice what the covariance term buys us. Dropping it — pretending \(\mathrm{Cov}(\widehat\beta_{p1}, \widehat\beta_{p2}) = 0\) — gives the wrong standard error, because in a polynomial the two coefficients are strongly correlated by construction.

title: Prediction Methods in the Linear Model
text:
Confidence intervals by end-point transformation
Either standard error can build the interval. Take the point estimate plus and minus 1.96 times the ML or the delta standard error, transforming the endpoints if the quantity is transformed:
\[
F(X\widehat\beta - 1.96\,se) \;\le\; F(X\widehat\beta) \;\le\; F(X\widehat\beta + 1.96\,se).
\]
The choice between the two matters only for a nonlinear quantity. An interval built on the linear predictor with the ML standard error and then transformed stays inside the natural bounds — a probability stays in \([0,1]\) — and comes out asymmetric. An interval built directly on the transformed quantity with the delta standard error is symmetric, and can fall outside those bounds. In OLS neither issue arises: \(F\) is the identity, so the interval is the symmetric \(\widehat y \pm 1.96\,se\) from the at-means figure, and the ML and delta standard errors are the same number to begin with. In a nonlinear model \(F\) is the link, and the difference between the two intervals is real.






Either standard error builds a confidence interval



Take the point estimate \(\pm\,1.96 \times se\) with either the ML or the delta standard error, transforming the endpoints if the quantity is transformed. The choice matters only for a nonlinear quantity: the ML interval (built on the linear scale, then transformed) stays in bounds and is asymmetric; the delta interval (built on the response) is symmetric and can leave the bounds. In OLS they coincide.

title: Prediction Methods in the Linear Model
section: Simulating the parameters — the expected value (confidence interval)
text:
Simulating the parameters — the expected value (confidence interval)
Treat \(\widehat\beta\) as the mean of a multivariate normal and \(\mathbf{V}\) as its variance, draw 10,000 coefficient vectors, and for each value of protest form the 10,000 linear predictions and take the percentiles.


code
B <- data.frame(rmvnorm(n = 10000, mean = coef(m1), sigma = vcov(m1)))
colnames(B) <- c("b0", "b_ra", "b_cw", "b_pro", "b_p1", "b_p2", "b_gdp")

sim.exp <- data.frame(lb = numeric(0), med = numeric(0), ub = numeric(0), pr = numeric(0))

for (i in seq(0, 37, 1)) {
  xbR <- quantile(B$b0 + B$b_ra*0 + B$b_cw*0 + B$b_pro*i +
                  B$b_p1*p1med + B$b_p2*p2med + B$b_gdp*gdpmed,
                  probs = c(.025, .5, .975))
  sim.exp[i + 1, 1:4] <- data.frame(t(xbR), i)
}

sim.exp %>% head()


        lb      med       ub pr
1 4.172945 5.420639 6.665929  0
2 4.475042 5.661991 6.850677  1
3 4.757268 5.904290 7.036988  2
4 5.029860 6.145498 7.259408  3
5 5.283568 6.387826 7.493155  4
6 5.516782 6.633641 7.752399  5


code
# ---- MORE EFFICIENT -----------------------------------
# Draw with MASS::mvrnorm, build all the linear predictions as one matrix
# multiply instead of looping, and skip the data.frame-row assignment:
#
#   sims <- MASS::mvrnorm(10000, coef(m1), vcov(m1))       # 10000 x k
#   grid <- seq(0, 37, 1)
#   Xg   <- model.matrix(~ lagRA + civilwar + lagprotest + p1 + p2 + loggdp,
#             data = data.frame(lagRA = 0, civilwar = 0, lagprotest = grid,
#                               p1 = p1med, p2 = p2med, loggdp = gdpmed))
#   XB   <- Xg %*% t(sims)                                 # length(grid) x 10000
#   ci   <- t(apply(XB, 1, quantile, c(.025, .5, .975)))   # one row per protest value
#
# WHY it's better: the matrix multiply replaces the loop and the fragile
# "i + 1" indexing, and building x'b from model.matrix means you never re-type
# the linear predictor by hand (where a dropped term hides). The manual loop is
# here because writing x'b out term-by-term makes it obvious what's being
# simulated.

title: Prediction Methods in the Linear Model
section: Simulating the quantity of interest — the predicted value (prediction interval)
text:
Simulating the quantity of interest — the predicted value (prediction interval)
Same draws of the parameters, but now we also add the fundamental uncertainty: for each simulated \(x\beta^{*}\) we add a disturbance draw \(\varepsilon^{*} \sim N(0, \widehat\sigma^2)\), where \(\widehat\sigma\) is the residual standard error, and take percentiles of the predicted value \(\widetilde y = x\beta^{*} + \varepsilon^{*}\).


code
sigma_hat <- sigma(m1)   # residual standard error -- the scatter around the line

sim.pred <- data.frame(lb = numeric(0), med = numeric(0), ub = numeric(0), pr = numeric(0))

for (i in seq(0, 37, 1)) {
  xstar <- B$b0 + B$b_pro*i + B$b_p1*p1med + B$b_p2*p2med + B$b_gdp*gdpmed  # binaries = 0
  ystar <- xstar + rnorm(length(xstar), mean = 0, sd = sigma_hat)          # add fundamental noise
  q <- quantile(ystar, probs = c(.025, .5, .975))
  sim.pred[i + 1, 1:4] <- data.frame(t(q), i)
}

sim.pred %>% head()


         lb      med       ub pr
1 -14.60143 5.400084 25.34124  0
2 -14.50950 5.690950 25.64214  1
3 -14.19927 6.174480 26.09840  2
4 -14.17129 5.990618 26.02624  3
5 -13.31731 6.505752 26.59697  4
6 -13.13051 6.534256 26.45667  5


Now put the two intervals on one plot, and overlay what predict() gives directly — the simulation should reproduce the analytic confidence and prediction intervals.


code
# analytic confidence and prediction intervals straight from predict()
check <- data.frame(lagprotest = oosdata$lagprotest,
  predict(m1, newdata = oosdata, interval = "confidence"),
  predict(m1, newdata = oosdata, interval = "prediction")) %>%
  rename(ci_lb = lwr, ci_ub = upr, pi_lb = lwr.1, pi_ub = upr.1)

ggplot() +
  # simulated prediction interval (wide) and confidence interval (narrow)
  geom_ribbon(data = sim.pred, aes(x = pr, ymin = lb, ymax = ub),
              fill = bu_lightgreen, alpha = .25) +
  geom_ribbon(data = sim.exp,  aes(x = pr, ymin = lb, ymax = ub),
              fill = bu_green, alpha = .35) +
  geom_line(data = sim.exp, aes(x = pr, y = med), color = bu_green, linewidth = 1) +
  # analytic checks, dashed, in dark ink so they read on the bands
  geom_line(data = check, aes(lagprotest, ci_lb), color = bu_black, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(data = check, aes(lagprotest, ci_ub), color = bu_black, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(data = check, aes(lagprotest, pi_lb), color = bu_black, linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_line(data = check, aes(lagprotest, pi_ub), color = bu_black, linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = bu_black, linewidth = .3) +
  annotate("text", x = 2, y = 11, label = "confidence interval\n(expected value)",
           hjust = 0, size = 3, color = bu_green) +
  annotate("text", x = 20, y = 26, label = "prediction interval\n(predicted value)",
           hjust = 0, size = 3, color = bu_black) +
  labs(title = "Two simulations: expected value vs. predicted value",
       subtitle = "solid/dark band = confidence interval; pale band = prediction interval; dashed/dotted = predict()",
       x = "Protests (t-1)", y = "Scarring torture") +
  theme_minimal()









The simulated bands land on the analytic ones — the dashed confidence bounds sit on the dark band, the dotted prediction bounds on the pale one. That is the payoff: the two “types of simulation” are not two techniques for the same quantity, they are two quantities. The confidence interval is our uncertainty about the average; the prediction interval is our uncertainty about a case, and it is much wider because it carries \(\widehat\sigma\).
And look where the prediction interval goes — below zero, for a variable that counts torture allegations and cannot be negative. OLS does not know scarring is a bounded count, so it puts real probability mass on impossible values. Nothing we do to the uncertainty technique fixes that; the fix is a different model, one whose link function keeps predictions non-negative (see count models in a few weeks)

title: Prediction Methods in the Linear Model
text:
Simulating combinations of binary variables
Simulation also lets us compare discrete scenarios and see the whole predicted distribution, not just a point and an interval. Here are the four combinations of restricted access and civil war, holding protest, Polity, and GDP at their medians, each as a density of simulated expected values.


code
# xb_scen() builds the simulated linear prediction for one access/war scenario.
# Its arguments are ra (restricted access, 0/1) and cw (civil war, 0/1). The
# other pieces come from the environment: the simulated coefficient columns
# B$... were drawn in the simulation chunk above, and the held medians
# promed/p1med/p2med/gdpmed in the estimation-sample chunk. It returns a full
# column of 10,000 simulated predictions. We call it four times, once per
# combination of ra and cw:
xb_scen <- function(ra, cw) {
  B$b0 + B$b_ra*ra + B$b_cw*cw + B$b_pro*promed +
  B$b_p1*p1med + B$b_p2*p2med + B$b_gdp*gdpmed
}

combos <- data.frame(ra0cw0 = xb_scen(0, 0), ra1cw0 = xb_scen(1, 0),
                     ra0cw1 = xb_scen(0, 1), ra1cw1 = xb_scen(1, 1))

ggplot(combos) +
  geom_density(aes(ra0cw0), fill = bu_green,      alpha = .3) +
  geom_density(aes(ra1cw0), fill = bu_lightgreen, alpha = .3) +
  geom_density(aes(ra0cw1), fill = bu_palegreen,  alpha = .3) +
  geom_density(aes(ra1cw1), fill = bu_grey,       alpha = .4) +
  annotate("text", x = 5.7,  y = .55, label = "open access,\nno civil war",   color = bu_black, size = 3) +
  annotate("text", x = 13.6, y = .45, label = "open access,\ncivil war",      color = bu_black, size = 3) +
  annotate("text", x = 16.8, y = .35, label = "restricted access,\nno civil war", color = bu_green, size = 3) +
  annotate("text", x = 24.7, y = .30, label = "restricted access,\ncivil war",    color = bu_black, size = 3) +
  labs(title = "Simulated expected scarring for four scenarios",
       x = "Expected scarring torture", y = "density") +
  theme_minimal()









Four clearly separated distributions. Restricted access shifts the whole distribution right by about eleven allegations; civil war by about eight; together they stack. And because we have the full simulated distribution, not just a point, we can read directly the probability that, say, a restricted-access country in civil war has higher expected scarring than an open one at peace — the overlap between two of these densities. That is the flexibility King, Tomz, and Wittenberg were after, and it is why simulation is the default when the quantity gets complicated.

title: Exercise #1 — Distributions, Simulation, and the Log-Likelihood (Answers)
text: Answer key for Exercise #1. The code is folded — open it to see how a piece was built.

title: Exercise #1 — Distributions, Simulation, and the Log-Likelihood (Answers)
text:
1. CDFs and PDFs

1. Please replicate this figure. What do the PDFs describe? What do the CDFs describe?



code
z  <- seq(-4, 4, length.out = 1000)
dz <- z[2] - z[1]

# Normal: density written by hand, then accumulated to get the CDF. The
# trapezoid rule averages consecutive heights. This is Phi(z) - Phi(-4); the
# mass below -4 is about .00003.
normal_pdf <- (1 / sqrt(2 * pi)) * exp(-z^2 / 2)
normal_cdf <- c(0, cumsum((head(normal_pdf, -1) + tail(normal_pdf, -1)) / 2 * dz))

dists <- tibble(
  z,
  Logistic = 1 / (1 + exp(-z)),
  Normal   = normal_cdf,
  Cauchy   = 0.5 + atan(z) / pi
) %>%
  pivot_longer(-z, names_to = "distribution", values_to = "cdf") %>%
  mutate(distribution = factor(distribution, levels = c("Logistic", "Normal", "Cauchy")))

densities <- tibble(
  z,
  Logistic = exp(-z) / (1 + exp(-z))^2,
  Normal   = normal_pdf,
  Cauchy   = 1 / (pi * (1 + z^2))
) %>%
  pivot_longer(-z, names_to = "distribution", values_to = "pdf") %>%
  mutate(distribution = factor(distribution, levels = c("Logistic", "Normal", "Cauchy")))

p_cdf <- ggplot(dists, aes(z, cdf, color = distribution, linetype = distribution)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_color_manual(values = series_colors) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = series_lines) +
  labs(title = "CDFs", x = expression(x*beta), y = "Pr(y = 1)",
       color = NULL, linetype = NULL) +
  theme_bu() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", plot.title = element_text(size = 12))

p_pdf <- ggplot(densities, aes(z, pdf, color = distribution, linetype = distribution)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_color_manual(values = series_colors) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = series_lines) +
  labs(title = "PDFs", x = expression(x*beta), y = "density",
       color = NULL, linetype = NULL) +
  theme_bu() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", plot.title = element_text(size = 12))

(p_cdf + p_pdf) +
  plot_layout(guides = "collect") +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "Logistic, normal, and Cauchy distributions",
    subtitle = "The CDF maps the linear predictor into [0,1]; the PDF is its slope",
    theme = theme_bu()
  ) &
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")








Figure 1





The CDF returns \(Pr(y = 1)\) at any value of \(x\beta\) — probability accumulated up to that point. It takes the real line, where \(x\beta\) lives, and squashes it into \([0,1]\), where a probability has to live.
The PDF is its derivative: how fast the probability changes at a given \(x\beta\). Tallest where the CDF is steepest, near zero in the tails where the CDF has flattened. A marginal effect is a slope, so this is the curve we want later.

title: Exercise #1 — Distributions, Simulation, and the Log-Likelihood (Answers)
text:
2. Three links

2. Please replicate this figure — it overlays the CDFs of the logistic, the complementary log-log (cloglog), and the log-log. Comment on the differences among the three.



code
links <- tibble(
  z,
  Logistic = 1 / (1 + exp(-z)),
  Cloglog  = 1 - exp(-exp(z)),
  Loglog   = exp(-exp(-z))
) %>%
  pivot_longer(-z, names_to = "link", values_to = "p") %>%
  mutate(link = factor(link, levels = c("Logistic", "Cloglog", "Loglog")))

ggplot(links, aes(z, p, color = link, linetype = link)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, color = bu_grey, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_color_manual(values = series_colors) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = series_lines) +
  labs(title = "Logistic, cloglog, and loglog CDFs",
       x = expression(x*beta), y = "Pr(y = 1)",
       color = NULL, linetype = NULL) +
  theme_bu() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")








Figure 2





The logistic is symmetric: \(\Lambda(-z) = 1 - \Lambda(z)\), so it crosses .5 at \(x\beta = 0\) and approaches 1 the way it approaches 0, run backwards. The cloglog and loglog are asymmetric, and they mirror each other rather than themselves. The cloglog, \(1 - \exp(-\exp(z))\), leaves zero gradually then rushes to one, crossing .5 at about \(-0.37\); the loglog does the reverse, crossing at about \(+0.37\).
That asymmetry is why we keep them. When ones are rare the action is in the bottom left, and that is where the three disagree most: a link that leaves zero slowly puts more mass down there than the logit does at the same \(x\beta\), one that leaves abruptly puts less. We are asking the data to tell very small probabilities apart, so the shape of that tail does real work. Hence the cloglog in rare-events work and in discrete-time hazards, where it is also the exact discrete-time analogue of a constant underlying hazard.

title: Exercise #1 — Distributions, Simulation, and the Log-Likelihood (Answers)
text:
3. Intercept shifts

3. Please replicate this figure — it overlays the logistic CDF with intercepts of \(-1\), \(0\), and \(+1\). Please describe what happens as the intercept changes. Then compare these intercept shifts to intercept shifts in the linear model: how are the two similar, and how are they different?



code
shifts <- tibble(
  z,
  `Intercept = -1` = 1 / (1 + exp(-(z - 1))),
  `Intercept = 0`  = 1 / (1 + exp(-z)),
  `Intercept = +1` = 1 / (1 + exp(-(z + 1)))
) %>%
  pivot_longer(-z, names_to = "intercept", values_to = "p") %>%
  mutate(intercept = factor(intercept,
                            levels = c("Intercept = -1", "Intercept = 0", "Intercept = +1")))

ggplot(shifts, aes(z, p, color = intercept, linetype = intercept)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, color = bu_grey, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_color_manual(values = series_colors) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = series_lines) +
  labs(title = "Logistic CDFs under intercept shifts",
       x = expression(x*beta), y = "Pr(y = 1)",
       color = NULL, linetype = NULL) +
  theme_bu() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")








Figure 3





Changing the intercept slides the curve sideways and does nothing else. Raise it by one and the curve moves one unit left, so the probability reaches one-half one unit earlier. Steepness and tails are identical across all three.
Same as the linear model: the intercept sets the level and leaves the slopes alone. Add \(c\) and every \(x\beta\) goes up by \(c\). On the \(x\beta\) scale the logit is linear, so the two behave identically there.
Different from the linear model on the scale we care about. In OLS the prediction is \(x\beta\), so a one-unit shift moves predicted \(y\) one unit, everywhere, for everybody. In the logit the prediction is \(\Lambda(x\beta)\), so the same shift moves the probability a lot in the steep middle and hardly at all in the flat tails — off the figure, about .23 at \(x\beta = 0\) and about .03 at \(x\beta = -4\). Constant on the \(x\beta\) scale, not constant on the probability scale. That is why a logit coefficient is not a marginal effect.

title: Exercise #1 — Distributions, Simulation, and the Log-Likelihood (Answers)
text:
4. The skewed logit (scobit)

4. Please replicate this figure — it overlays the skewed logit (scobit) CDF at shape parameters \(\alpha = 1\), \(\alpha = 2\), and \(\alpha = 0.5\). Please describe what happens as the shape parameter changes. How are these curves similar to, and different from, the logistic CDF in question 3?



code
scobit <- tibble(
  z,
  `alpha = 1`   = 1 / (1 + exp(-z))^1,
  `alpha = 2`   = 1 / (1 + exp(-z))^2,
  `alpha = 0.5` = 1 / (1 + exp(-z))^0.5
) %>%
  pivot_longer(-z, names_to = "shape", values_to = "p") %>%
  mutate(shape = factor(shape, levels = c("alpha = 1", "alpha = 2", "alpha = 0.5")))

ggplot(scobit, aes(z, p, color = shape, linetype = shape)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, color = bu_grey, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_color_manual(values = series_colors,
                     labels = c(expression(alpha == 1), expression(alpha == 2),
                                expression(alpha == 0.5))) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = series_lines,
                        labels = c(expression(alpha == 1), expression(alpha == 2),
                                   expression(alpha == 0.5))) +
  labs(title = "Skewed logit (scobit) CDFs",
       x = expression(x*beta), y = "Pr(y = 1)",
       color = NULL, linetype = NULL) +
  theme_bu() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")








Figure 4





At \(\alpha = 1\) the scobit is the logit — raise \((1 + e^{-z})^{-1}\) to the first power and you have written \(\Lambda(z)\). The logit is the special case, so “is the logit good enough here?” becomes a hypothesis about a single number rather than a matter of taste.
Move \(\alpha\) off 1 and the curve bends, which is a different operation from question 3. An intercept shift is a rigid translation — same curve, new location. Changing \(\alpha\) deforms it: the steepest point moves off \(Pr(y = 1) = .5\) and the tails stop mirroring each other. At \(\alpha = 2\) the curve hugs zero longer and is steepest below .5; at \(\alpha = 0.5\) it lifts off early and is steepest above .5.
Nagler’s motivation: the logit forces the largest marginal effects to land at \(Pr(y = 1) = .5\), for everyone, always, by construction. That is an assumption, and a strong one. If the people most responsive to \(x\) are not the ones sitting at fifty-fifty — for turnout, the argument is that they are not — you want that location estimated rather than imposed. That is what \(\alpha\) does.

title: Exercise #1 — Distributions, Simulation, and the Log-Likelihood (Answers)
text:
5. Simulate a binary outcome

5. Please write code that simulates data for a binary \(y\) variable from the equation \(x\beta = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2\), with \(\beta_0 = -1\), \(\beta_1 = 0.5\), and \(\beta_2 = -0.5\), with a logit link. Let \(x_1\) be continuous and \(x_2\) be binary. The output should be a data frame of 1,000 observations containing a binary \(y\), a constant, and the two \(x\) variables.

The data-generating process, stated before any code is written:
\[
\begin{aligned}
x_{1i} &\sim \text{Normal}(0,1), \qquad x_{2i} \sim \text{Bernoulli}(0.5) \\
x_i\beta &= -1 + 0.5\,x_{1i} - 0.5\,x_{2i} \\
\pi_i &= \Lambda(x_i\beta) \;=\; \frac{1}{1 + e^{-x_i\beta}} \\
y_i &\sim \text{Bernoulli}(\pi_i)
\end{aligned}
\]
The third line is the link: take \(x_i\beta\), free to be any real number, and hand back a probability. Write \(\Phi(x_i\beta)\) instead and you have simulated a probit; write \(1 - \exp(-\exp(x_i\beta))\) and you have a cloglog. Nothing above or below that line changes.
The last two lines are the model. The systematic part produces a probability, one per observation; the stochastic part turns it into a zero or a one with a coin weighted by \(\pi_i\). Two observations with identical \(x\)’s get identical \(\pi\)’s and can still get different \(y\)’s. That is why we estimate \(\pi\) rather than \(y\).


code
set.seed(8675309)

n  <- 1000
x1 <- rnorm(n)                # continuous
x2 <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.5)       # binary

xb <- -1 + 0.5 * x1 - 0.5 * x2

# The logit link, written out rather than calling plogis(). Call it `pr`, not
# `pi` -- in R, `pi` is already 3.14159..., and overwriting it breaks any later
# line that needs the real one.
pr <- 1 / (1 + exp(-xb))
y  <- rbinom(n, 1, pr)        # the coin flip: y is random even given pr

sim <- tibble(y, const = 1, x1, x2)

c(n = n, share_ones = round(mean(sim$y), 3), mean_pr = round(mean(pr), 3))


         n share_ones    mean_pr 
  1000.000      0.239      0.236 


About 0.239 of the observations are ones, close to the mean of the \(\pi_i\)’s, 0.236, as it should be. Both sit below one-half, which is what the \(-1\) intercept gets us: at \(x_1 = 0\), \(x_2 = 0\) the probability is \(\Lambda(-1) = 0.269\).
We also have the true \(\beta = (-1, 0.5, -0.5)\), because we chose it. In real data we never do, which is why simulated data is the place to test an estimator like this.

title: Exercise #1 — Distributions, Simulation, and the Log-Likelihood (Answers)
text:
6. The likelihood and log-likelihood

6. Please write (in proper math notation, not code) the likelihood and log-likelihood functions for a binary \(y\) variable using the logit as the link function. Describe the parts of the log-likelihood and what each is doing.

Start with the general form; it is the same for every binary model, and only one piece changes. Each observation contributes the probability of the outcome we observed for it: \(\pi_i\) when \(y_i = 1\), \(1 - \pi_i\) when \(y_i = 0\). Putting \(y_i\) and \(1 - y_i\) in the exponents writes that as one term — one exponent is always zero, so one factor always drops out.
\[
\begin{aligned}
L(\beta \mid y) &= \prod_{i=1}^{n} \pi_i^{\,y_i}\,(1 - \pi_i)^{\,1 - y_i} \\
\ell(\beta \mid y) &= \ln L(\beta \mid y)
                    = \sum_{i=1}^{n}\Big[\, y_i \ln \pi_i + (1 - y_i)\ln(1 - \pi_i)\Big]
\end{aligned}
\]
with \(\pi_i = F(x_i\beta)\) for whatever link \(F\) we chose. For the logit, \(\pi_i = \Lambda(x_i\beta) = 1/(1 + e^{-x_i\beta})\), and
\[
\begin{aligned}
L(\beta \mid y) &= \prod_{i=1}^{n} \Lambda(x_i\beta)^{\,y_i}\,
                   \big[1 - \Lambda(x_i\beta)\big]^{\,1 - y_i} \\
\ell(\beta \mid y) &= \sum_{i=1}^{n} \Big[\, y_i \ln \Lambda(x_i\beta)
                      + (1 - y_i)\ln\big(1 - \Lambda(x_i\beta)\big) \Big]
\end{aligned}
\]
Note where the link sits — inside both terms and nowhere else. Swap \(\Lambda\) for \(\Phi\) and you have the probit; exchange it for \(1 - \exp(-\exp(\cdot))\) and you have the cloglog.

title: Exercise #1 — Distributions, Simulation, and the Log-Likelihood (Answers)
text:
7. The log-likelihood in R

7. Please write the log-likelihood function from above in R code, as a function. It should take as arguments a vector of parameters, a matrix of \(X\) variables, and a \(y\) variable, and return a single number (the log-likelihood). Using the data from question #5 for \(X\) and \(y\), evaluate the log-likelihood at the true \(\beta\)’s from question #5; the \(\beta\)’s from a glm logit of the data and equation from question #5; \(\beta\) values of 0, 0, 0; and \(\beta\) values of 1, -.5, .5. Present the log-likelihoods in a professional table and comment.



code
# Build xb, transform it through the link to get probabilities, sum the two
# terms. Three arguments in, one number out.
logit_ll <- function(beta, X, y) {
  xb <- as.vector(X %*% beta)
  p  <- 1 / (1 + exp(-xb))
  sum(y * log(p) + (1 - y) * log(1 - p))
}

X <- cbind(const = 1, x1 = sim$x1, x2 = sim$x2)

b_hat <- coef(glm(y ~ x1 + x2, family = binomial(link = "logit"), data = sim))

ll_table <- tibble(
  `beta` = c("truth (-1, 0.5, -0.5)",
             "glm logit estimate",
             "all zeros (0, 0, 0)",
             "sign-flipped (1, -0.5, 0.5)"),
  `log-likelihood` = c(
    logit_ll(c(-1, 0.5, -0.5), X, sim$y),
    logit_ll(b_hat,            X, sim$y),
    logit_ll(c(0, 0, 0),       X, sim$y),
    logit_ll(c(1, -0.5, 0.5),  X, sim$y)
  )
)

knitr::kable(ll_table, digits = 3, align = "lr",
             caption = "The logit log-likelihood evaluated at four values of beta")



The logit log-likelihood evaluated at four values of beta


beta
log-likelihood




truth (-1, 0.5, -0.5)
-521.555


glm logit estimate
-521.374


all zeros (0, 0, 0)
-693.147


sign-flipped (1, -0.5, 0.5)
-1296.000





glm returns (-1.014, 0.526, -0.434) when the true parameters are \((-1, 0.5, -0.5)\).
The function prefers the glm estimate — highest of the four, with the truth second by about a tenth of a point. The estimate beats the truth, which might suprise you, but it shouldn’t. The log-likelihood is a statement about this sample, and \(\hat\beta\) is by construction the value that makes these thousand observations most probable. The true \(\beta\) generated the sample but does not fit it best, because the sample carries noise too. Re-run with a different seed and \(\hat\beta\) moves around the truth; let \(n\) grow and the two will converge.
Note that we have not maximized anything. We wrote a function and evaluated it at four points, and picking the best of four is not estimation. Finding the \(\beta\) that beats every other \(\beta\) is the problem, and it is what maximization is for.

section: 8. Logit and probit on the CES data
text:
8. Logit and probit on the CES data

8. Please estimate logit and probit models predicting vote choice as a function of whatever variables you think are relevant. Present a professional table of the estimates in side-by-side columns and discuss. Explain your thinking about the models — why did you include these variables, and what did you expect?

Binary vote choice — Biden = 1, Trump = 0, everyone else missing — predicted by age, an indicator for white respondents, and a pro-choice indicator.
Why these three. The abortion item is the best available proxy for the cultural dimension that dominated the 2020 vote, so I expect the largest effect by far, positive. Race has been the most durable cleavage in American voting for fifty years, so white respondents less likely to vote Biden. Age I include as a control and as a continuous variable over which to plot predictions.
We do not drop the missing cases by hand; glm does the listwise deletion, because we need to recover exactly which rows it used when we predict in question 10.


code
ces <- read_csv(here::here("data", "ces.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)

# Recode: a binary vote, and two binary predictors. Anything that isn't a Biden

cesa <- ces %>%
  mutate(
    vote  = case_when(votechoice == "Joe Biden (Democrat)"         ~ 1,
                      votechoice == "Donald J. Trump (Republican)" ~ 0,
                      .default = NA_real_),
    white = if_else(race == "White", 1, 0),
    pro   = if_else(prochoice == "Support", 1, 0)
  )

m_logit  <- glm(vote ~ age + white + pro, family = binomial(link = "logit"),
                data = cesa)
m_probit <- glm(vote ~ age + white + pro, family = binomial(link = "probit"),

modal <- function(x) as.numeric(names(which.max(table(x))))

title: Exercise #1 — Distributions, Simulation, and the Log-Likelihood (Answers)
text:
9. Odds ratios

9. Please compute odds ratios for the variables of interest in the logit model, and discuss them. What do they tell you?

Exponentiating a logit coefficient turns it into an odds ratio, and it works only for the logit, because the logit link is the log of the odds:
\[
\ln\!\left(\frac{\pi_i}{1 - \pi_i}\right) = x_i\beta
\qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad
\frac{\pi_i}{1 - \pi_i} = e^{x_i\beta}.
\]
Increase \(x_k\) by one unit and the odds get multiplied by \(e^{\beta_k}\). The intervals below exponentiate the endpoints of the interval on the coefficient scale — the same end-point logic as the predicted probabilities in question 10, for the same reason: form the interval where the sampling distribution is symmetric, then transform.


code
b  <- coef(m_logit)
se <- sqrt(diag(vcov(m_logit)))

tibble(
  term       = names(b),
  coefficient = b,
  `odds ratio` = exp(b),
  lower       = exp(b - 1.96 * se),
  upper       = exp(b + 1.96 * se)
) %>%
  filter(term != "(Intercept)") %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3)))


# A tibble: 3 x 5
  term  coefficient `odds ratio`  lower  upper
  <chr>       <dbl>        <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>
1 age        -0.014        0.986  0.984  0.987
2 white      -1.08         0.339  0.318  0.362
3 pro         2.85        17.3   16.5   18.2  


Read them as multipliers on the odds, with 1 as the null value rather than 0. Pro-choice multiplies the odds of a Biden vote by about 17; white respondents are 66% less likely to vote for Biden than non-whites (1-.339).

title: Exercise #1 — Distributions, Simulation, and the Log-Likelihood (Answers)
text:
10. Predicted probabilities and intervals

10. Please generate predicted probabilities and intervals from both models and present professional plots — separately, one plot for each model. For the logit, please use average effects; for the probit, please use at-mean effects. For both, the \(x\) axis should be a continuous variable, and each plot should show two lines, one for each value of a binary variable of interest. Please write the code for these yourself — that is, don’t call a package that produces the predictions or marginal effects for you. Write a couple of sentences describing/interpreting your figures (as you would in a journal article).

Both confidence intervals come from the delta method, in the form the prediction notes give it:
\[
\mathrm{Var}\!\left[F(x\widehat\beta)\right] \;=\; f(x\widehat\beta)^2\;\mathbf{x}'\mathbf{V}\mathbf{x},
\]
with \(F\) the link and \(f\) its derivative — the link’s PDF. Notice that the standard error of a predicted probability is the standard error of the linear prediction, scaled by the height of the PDF at that point. The first piece is one you already have — it is \(\sqrt{\mathrm{diag}(\mathbf{XVX}')}\), the same ML standard error predict() reports for \(x\widehat\beta\). The second is \(\phi(x\widehat\beta)\) for the probit and \(\lambda(x\widehat\beta) = \pi(1-\pi)\) for the logit.
The average effects plot needs one more step because we’re computing the average over the entire sample. There we compute a probability for every respondent and average them, so there is no single row and no single height — every observation has its own. The PDF cannot come out front as a scalar so must be inside the average computation.
\[
\bar{\mathbf{g}} \;=\; \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} f(x_i\widehat\beta)\,\mathbf{x}_i,
\qquad
se = \sqrt{\bar{\mathbf{g}}'\,\mathbf{V}\,\bar{\mathbf{g}}}.
\]

Logit: average effects


code
# Reconstruct the estimation sample: na.action() returns the rows glm dropped
# for missingness, so `esample` is exactly the data the model was fit on.
cesa$used <- TRUE
cesa$used[na.action(m_logit)] <- FALSE
esample <- cesa %>% filter(used == TRUE)

b <- coef(m_logit)      # beta-hat
V <- vcov(m_logit)      # its estimated sampling variance -- the delta method's input

age_grid <- seq(20, 90, by = 5)

# Average effects with a delta-method interval, in four steps.
#   quantity:  pbar(beta) = (1/n) * sum_i Lambda(x_i beta)
#   gradient:  g = (1/n) * sum_i lambda(x_i b) * x_i, one per coefficient
# lambda() is the logistic PDF, so each row of X is weighted by how responsive
# that respondent's own probability is.
avg_delta <- function(a, pro_value) {
  cf      <- esample            # counterfactual COPY -- never overwrite esample
  cf$age  <- a                  # (1) everyone is this age ...
  cf$pro  <- pro_value          #     ... and holds this abortion position

  X    <- model.matrix(~ age + white + pro, data = cf)
  xb   <- as.vector(X %*% b)
  p    <- plogis(xb)            # every respondent's predicted probability
  dens <- p * (1 - p)           # lambda(xb): the logistic PDF, from question 1

  g  <- colMeans(dens * X)                       # (2) gradient of the average
  se <- sqrt(as.vector(t(g) %*% V %*% g))        # (3) delta-method SE: g' V g

  tibble(age = a, pro = pro_value,
         p  = mean(p),
         lb = mean(p) - 1.96 * se,               # (4) symmetric, probability scale
         ub = mean(p) + 1.96 * se)
}

avg_effects <- map_dfr(c(0, 1), function(pv) map_dfr(age_grid, avg_delta, pro_value = pv)) %>%
  mutate(pro = factor(pro, levels = c(0, 1),
                      labels = c("Opposes abortion rights", "Pro-choice")))

ggplot(avg_effects, aes(age, p, color = pro, fill = pro)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lb, ymax = ub), alpha = 0.3, linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  labs(title = "Predicted probability of a Biden vote, by age and abortion position",
       subtitle = "Logit average effects, 95% delta-method intervals",
       x = "Age", y = "Pr(Biden vote)", color = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  scale_color_manual(values = bu_two) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = bu_two) +
  theme_bu() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")











Probit: at-means effects
One constructed respondent instead of the whole sample, every covariate we are not varying held at its central tendency — the mode for white, since the mean of a dummy describes nobody. The delta method here is the same calculation with \(n = 1\), so we can check it against predict(type = "response", se.fit = TRUE), which computes this standard error by this method. I recommend using the se.fit = TRUE standard errors in at-mean predictions to save yourselves the trouble of computing them, but want you to see how and to have code with which to do it. Please note that this packaged method will not make sense with average predictions.


code
b_p <- coef(m_probit)
V_p <- vcov(m_probit)

# Central tendencies from the estimation sample, so they describe what the model saw.
white_mode <- as.numeric(names(sort(table(esample$white), decreasing = TRUE))[1])

# Out-of-sample data: ONE respondent, walked across the age grid at each value of pro.
mem <- expand_grid(age = age_grid, pro = c(0, 1)) %>%
  mutate(white = white_mode)

# One row per scenario, so the PDF is a scalar and factors out:
#   se(p-hat) = phi(xb) * sqrt(x' V x)
# That second factor is the ML standard error of the linear prediction.
Xm     <- model.matrix(~ age + white + pro, data = mem)
xb     <- as.vector(Xm %*% b_p)
se_lin <- sqrt(diag(Xm %*% V_p %*% t(Xm)))          # (2) SE of xb
se     <- dnorm(xb) * se_lin                        # (3) scaled by the PDF

at_means <- mem %>%
  mutate(p  = pnorm(xb),
         lb = pnorm(xb) - 1.96 * se,                # (4)
         ub = pnorm(xb) + 1.96 * se,
         pro = factor(pro, levels = c(0, 1),
                      labels = c("Opposes abortion rights", "Pro-choice")))

# Check the hand calculation against R's. stopifnot() is silent when it passes
# and stops the render when it fails.
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(se, predict(m_probit, newdata = mem, type = "response",
                                       se.fit = TRUE)$se.fit,
                           check.attributes = FALSE))) 




code
ggplot(at_means, aes(age, p, color = pro, fill = pro)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lb, ymax = ub), alpha = 0.3, linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  labs(title = "Predicted probability of a Biden vote, by age and abortion position",
       subtitle = "Probit at-means effects, 95% delta-method intervals",
       x = "Age", y = "Pr(Biden vote)", color = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  scale_color_manual(values = bu_two) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = bu_two) +
  theme_bu() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")









The two plots look almost the same, and they should — two links on the same binomial likelihood, and these predictions never get near the tails of the CDFs where the links part ways.
The vertical distance between the two lines is the effect of the abortion itemin probability at each age — about .591 at age 20, .586 at age 90. Nearly constant, because over this age range \(x\beta\) moves too little for the lines to curve much at all. Out in the flat tails the same shift would be worth a fraction of that.


What you would actually write
This text could refer to either of the plots, though I’ll talk about the logit:

Figure 1 plots the predictions from the logit model. The most striking effect is the difference in vote choice depending on whether a voter is pro-choice or not. Pro-choice voters are 55 to 59 percentage points more likely to vote for Biden across the range of age. Vote choice varies relatively little across age, a total of about a 17 point decline over the entire range. Both of the predictions lines remain strictly above (pro-choice) or below (anti-abortion) the \(Pr(y=.5)\) threshold, suggesting even a 17 point change (over 70 years) is not likely to shift a hypothetical voter from one candidate to the other. The mild negative slope suggests both groups become slightly less likely to support Biden as age increases; older voters mildly prefer Trump in this particular election.

title: Exercise #3 — Build Your Own Estimator
text:
You have built the binomial machine — a likelihood, a parameterization, a link, a maximizer. It does not care what \(y\) is: swap the distribution and the link and every other part stays put. Today you’ll swap them out, and you build the whole thing by hand before using a canned optimizer.
We’ll do this working in groups and using real data. I am not telling you which distribution to use and I am not writing the log-likelihood for you. Look at \(y\); the likelihood notes provide guidance you’ll need.






What you do



Nine chunks are marked TODO. Fill them, then render. If it renders and the self-check tables are all TRUE, you built it. That is the whole exercise.
Until you fill them in, the test tables below read FALSE and the results are empty. That is what an unfinished build looks like, not a broken page.
The TODO chunks are yours. Nothing else is. The setup, the test tables, and the self-check are the file’s, and they are what tell you whether the thing works — editing them to turn a FALSE into a TRUE only removes your own instrument. If a check is red and you are sure your code is right, come find me.


To get your own copy, run this in the console — it lands in your working directory under the right name:
download.file("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/clavedark/MLEfall26/main/buildtemplate26.qmd",
              "buildtemplate26.qmd")






The recipe




Observe \(y\); consider its distribution; write down its PDF/PMF.
Write the joint probability of the data.
Rewrite as a likelihood.
Simplify — take logs.
Parameterize — make the distribution’s parameter a function of \(x\beta\).
Choose a link that respects the parameter’s bounds.

title: Exercise #3 — Build Your Own Estimator
text:
Why \(\beta = \mathbf{0}\) makes this easy
Set every coefficient to zero so that \(x_i\beta = 0\) for every observation, and so \(\lambda_i = e^0 = 1\) — the rate is 1 for every case. Put that into the three expressions you derived in Step 2 and each one collapses to something simple:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\ell(\mathbf{0}) &= \sum_{i=1}^{n}\big[\,y_i(x_i\beta) - e^{x_i\beta} - \ln(y_i!)\,\big]
   \;=\; \sum_{i=1}^{n}\big[\,0 - 1 - \ln(y_i!)\,\big]
   \;=\; -n - \sum_{i=1}^{n}\ln(y_i!) \\[6pt]
s(\mathbf{0}) &= X'(y - \lambda) \;=\; X'(y - \mathbf{1}) \\[6pt]
H(\mathbf{0}) &= -X'\Lambda X \;=\; -X'IX \;=\; -X'X .
\end{aligned}
\]
Every one of those is a single line of R, and none needs the general case (coded in your functions): the log-likelihood loses its first two terms because \(y_i \cdot 0 = 0\) and \(e^0 = 1\); the score is the fitted values replaced by a column of ones; the Hessian’s weight matrix becomes the identity and drops out.

                                   length(mle_score(b0, X, y)) == k,
                                   identical(dim(mle_hessian(b0, X, y)), c(k, k))),
  `matches direct calculation` = c(isTRUE(all.equal(mle_ll(b0, X, y), ll_direct)),
                                   isTRUE(all.equal(as.vector(mle_score(b0, X, y)),
                                                    as.vector(score_direct))),
                                   isTRUE(all.equal(as.vector(mle_hessian(b0, X, y)),
                                                    as.vector(hess_direct))))
) %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "Each piece at beta = 0, against the closed form")

One more test. Everything above is evaluated at \(\beta = \mathbf{0}\), where the parameter is 1 for every case — so a function that is only correct at zero passes it. A Hessian that drops the weight entirely is exactly right at \(\beta = \mathbf{0}\) and wrong everywhere else, and the table above will not notice.
So test the pieces against each other, away from zero. Your score is the derivative of your log-likelihood, and your Hessian is the derivative of your score. A numerical derivative of one should reproduce the other, at any \(\beta\) you like, and no closed form is needed.


code
b1 <- c(1, 0.5, 0.5, 0.05, 0.1)     # any beta that is not zero

# central difference: ( f(b + e) - f(b - e) ) / 2e, one column per coefficient
numderiv <- function(f, b) {
  sapply(seq_along(b), function(j) {
    e <- rep(0, length(b)); e[j] <- 1e-5
    (f(b + e, X, y) - f(b - e, X, y)) / 2e-5
  })
}

tibble(
  check = c("mle_score matches the numerical derivative of mle_ll",
            "mle_hessian matches the numerical derivative of mle_score"),
  pass  = c(isTRUE(all.equal(as.vector(mle_score(b1, X, y)),
                             as.vector(numderiv(mle_ll, b1)), tolerance = 1e-4)),
            isTRUE(all.equal(as.vector(mle_hessian(b1, X, y)),
                             as.vector(numderiv(mle_score, b1)), tolerance = 1e-4)))
) %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "The same three pieces, tested away from zero")



The same three pieces, tested away from zero

If the first table is green and this one is not, the piece it names works at zero but at no other value — look at the weight.
Two things to check by eye before you trust the tables. Is the score anywhere near zero? It should not be — \(\beta = \mathbf{0}\) is a long way from the maximum and the score only vanishes at the top; what you are testing here is arithmetic, not optimality. And the diagonal of your Hessian should be negative everywhere. Say in a sentence why that has to be true at a maximum, and what a positive element would do to your standard errors.
(The table compares with all.equal rather than == because these are floating-point numbers, and wraps it in isTRUE because all.equal returns a description of the difference rather than FALSE when things do not match. as.vector on both sides strips names and dimensions so only the numbers are compared.)

title: MLE Syllabus
text:
Seminar Description
This 4 credit hour seminar is a survey of maximum likelihood methods and their applications to empirical political questions. It presumes students have a detailed and intuitive knowledge of least squares, probability theory, basic skills in scalar and matrix algebra, and a basic understanding of calculus. The course will deal mainly in understanding the principles of maximum likelihood estimation, under what conditions we move away from least squares, and what particular models are appropriate given observed data. The seminar will focus on application and interpretation of ML models and linking theory to statistical models. The course emphasizes coding and data viz in R.
The class meets one time per week for three hours. My office hours are designed to be homework help hours where I’ll work in the grad lab with any of you who are working on the exercises. The most productive pathway for this class is for you to get in the habit of working together, and those office hours are a good time for this.

title: MLE Syllabus
text:
Course Purpose
This seminar fulfills the advanced quantitative methods requirement in the Ph.D. curriculum. The method of maximum likelihood underlies a majority of quantitative models in Political Science; this class teaches students to be astute consumers of such models, and how to implement and interpret ML models. These are crucial skills for dissertations in Political Science, and for producing publishable quantitative research.

title: MLE Syllabus
text:
Learning Objectives
Students will encounter an array of maximum likelihood models in this course. By the end of the course, students will have mastered the theory of maximum likelihood sufficient to write and program likelihood functions in ; they will be able to choose, estimate, and interpret appropriate models, model specifications, and model evaluation tools given their data; and they will be able to produce sophisticated quantities of interest (e.g. predicted probabilities, expected values, confidence intervals) via a variety of techniques including simulation and end point transformation. Students will also be able to present model findings verbally and graphically.

Reading
The reading material for the course is important because it often demonstrates application of various MLE models; seeing how folks apply these and how they motivate their applications is really informative, something you cannot miss. We often won’t directly discuss the readings, but don’t let that imply they’re not important. If I get the sense we’re not keeping up with reading, expect the syllabus to change to incorporate quizzes or other accountability measures.
Reading for the course will consist of several books and articles (listed by week below). The books listed below also have Amazon links - you’ll find most of these cheaper used online.

title: MLE Syllabus
text:
Course Policies

Attendance
Attendance is expected, and is essential if you’re to succeed in this class.


Academic Integrity
Ideas are the currency in academic exchange, so acknowledging where ideas come from is important. Acknowledging the sources of ideas also helps us identify an idea’s lineage which can be important for understanding how that line of thought has developed, and toward promoting future growth. As graduate students, you should have a good understanding of academic honesty and best practices. Here are details of Binghamton’s honesty policy.


Artificial Intelligence and Coding Tools
Generative AI can act as an incredible accelerator for research, for coding and data management in particular. Such tools are only as useful as your own mastery of coding, data management, and modeling.
Do you need to be able to write code when AI can do it for you? Yes. Three reasons:

Understanding. Code and the act of coding are the windows to seeing and understanding data, models, and predictions — how data produce models, which in turn produce predictions. Code is an explicit connection between a data matrix and a model, and facilitates your understanding of the what the model produces. AI can’t hand you that understanding; you build it by doing the work yourself.
Criticism. AI will produce code. If you can code, you can read it, critique it, and evaluate its output to judge whether it’s right. If you can’t code, you can’t do any of that — you’re left trusting output you have no way to check.
Inquiry. If you don’t understand the code, you probably don’t understand the data and the model, and you’ll not write a very good query to the AI in the first place. AI is only as good as its user. You should always know things the AI does not, in terms of your argument, your data, your model, and your code.

So here is the policy for this course. Do not use generative AI to produce code. If you get stuck coding, you may use AI to get unstuck - this is equivalent to consulting “stackexchange” or “stackoverflow” to solve code problems and get unstuck. Anytime you consult AI, you must cite and annotate it specifically: what you asked, why you asked it, and which parts of your code came from the AI. To this end, expect assessment where I ask you to show that you understand the data, code, models, and predictions you are producing. A bot can’t fake that understanding.
You should not use generative AI tools for writing in this course. Learning to express your ideas about politics, about causal relations, about data and models, and explaining your findings are core skills for the Ph.D. Please learn to do these things without any use of generative AI.

title: Exercise #2 — Write the Maximizer (Answers)
text:
1. Simulate a known truth

1. Simulate \(n = 2{,}000\) observations of a binary \(y\) from a logit DGP with one continuous covariate, one binary covariate, and an intercept.

\[
\begin{aligned}
x_{1i} &\sim \text{Normal}(0,1), \qquad x_{2i} \sim \text{Bernoulli}(0.5) \\
x_i\beta &= -0.5 + 0.75\,x_{1i} - 1\,x_{2i} \\
\pi_i &= \Lambda(x_i\beta) \;=\; \frac{1}{1 + e^{-x_i\beta}} \\
y_i &\sim \text{Bernoulli}(\pi_i)
\end{aligned}
\]


code
set.seed(20260902)

n     <- 2000
truth <- c(`(Intercept)` = -0.5, x1 = 0.75, x2 = -1)

x1 <- rnorm(n)
x2 <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.5)

xb <- truth[1] + truth[2] * x1 + truth[3] * x2
pr <- 1 / (1 + exp(-xb))
y  <- rbinom(n, 1, pr)

sim <- tibble(y, x1, x2)
X   <- model.matrix(~ x1 + x2, data = sim)

c(n = n, share_ones = round(mean(sim$y), 3))


         n share_ones 
     2e+03      3e-01 


About 0.3 of the observations are ones.

title: Exercise #2 — Write the Maximizer (Answers)
section: 2–4. The log-likelihood, the score, and the Hessian
text:
2–4. The log-likelihood, the score, and the Hessian

2. logit_ll(beta, X, y). 3. logit_score(beta, X, y). 4. logit_hessian(beta, X, y).

\[
\ell(\beta) = \sum_{i=1}^{n}\Big[y_i \ln \pi_i + (1-y_i)\ln(1-\pi_i)\Big],
\qquad
\nabla\ell(\beta) = X'(y - \pi),
\qquad
H(\beta) = -X'WX,
\]
with \(\pi_i = \Lambda(x_i\beta)\) and \(W = \mathrm{diag}\big(\pi_i(1-\pi_i)\big)\).


code
# Build xb, transform to probabilities, sum the two terms. One number out.
logit_ll <- function(beta, X, y) {
  p <- 1 / (1 + exp(-as.vector(X %*% beta)))
  sum(y * log(p) + (1 - y) * log(1 - p))
}

# The score, X'(y - pi). Comes back as a k-vector, one per coefficient.
logit_score <- function(beta, X, y) {
  p <- 1 / (1 + exp(-as.vector(X %*% beta)))
  as.vector(t(X) %*% (y - p))
}

# The Hessian, -X'WX, with W = diag(pi(1-pi)). `X * w` scales each column of X
# by the weights, which is what X'WX needs and avoids building the n x n W.
logit_hessian <- function(beta, X, y) {
  p <- 1 / (1 + exp(-as.vector(X %*% beta)))
  -t(X) %*% (X * (p * (1 - p)))
}


The X * (p * (1 - p)) construction is the one place students reliably get stuck. \(W\) is an \(n \times n\) diagonal matrix in the notation, and writing it that way works on the simulated data and then tries to allocate a 43,000 × 43,000 matrix on the CES data. Recognizing that \(X'WX\) only ever uses the diagonal — so the weights can scale the rows of \(X\) directly — is the practical version of the same formula.
Why the Hessian is \(k \times k\). Because the coefficients are not estimated separately. The off-diagonal element for \(\beta_1\) and \(\beta_2\) says how the slope in one direction changes as you move in the other — how much what we learn about one coefficient depends on the value of another. That is what makes a single Newton step update the whole vector at once rather than each coefficient on its own, and it is why the inverse of \(-H\) has covariances in it and not just variances.

title: Exercise #2 — Write the Maximizer (Answers)
text:
5. The estimator

5. fit_logit(X, y, tol, maxit) — start, compute score and Hessian, step, record, check, then standard errors.

The update rule, from the maximization notes:
\[
\beta^{(t+1)} \;=\; \beta^{(t)} + (X'WX)^{-1}X'(y-\pi)
\;=\; \beta^{(t)} - H\big(\beta^{(t)}\big)^{-1}\nabla\ell\big(\beta^{(t)}\big).
\]


code
fit_logit <- function(X, y, tol = 1e-8, maxit = 50) {

  beta      <- rep(0, ncol(X))   # start at zero
  hist      <- list()
  converged <- FALSE

  for (it in 1:maxit) {

    g <- logit_score(beta, X, y)
    H <- logit_hessian(beta, X, y)

    # solve(-H, g) solves the system directly, rather than forming solve(-H)
    # and multiplying. Faster, and better conditioned.
    step <- solve(-H, g)

    # Record before stepping, so row `it` describes the guess just evaluated.
    hist[[it]] <- c(iter     = it,
                    loglik   = logit_ll(beta, X, y),
                    max_grad = max(abs(g)),
                    max_step = max(abs(step)))

    beta <- beta + step

    if (max(abs(step)) < tol) { converged <- TRUE; break }
  }

  # The loop's H was computed one step before the final beta, so recompute the
  # curvature at beta-hat.
  H_hat <- logit_hessian(beta, X, y)
  V     <- solve(-H_hat)          # -H is the observed information

  list(coef       = setNames(beta, colnames(X)),
       se         = setNames(sqrt(diag(V)), colnames(X)),
       vcov       = V,
       loglik     = logit_ll(beta, X, y),
       iterations = it,
       converged  = converged,
       history    = as_tibble(do.call(rbind, hist)))
}


Starting values. Zero, which says every coefficient is null and every \(\pi_i\) is one-half. The binomial log-likelihood is globally concave, so there is one hill and one top and it does not matter much where we start — but zero is the honest default, and it is the value whose log-likelihood we can compute by hand as a check.
Convergence. The assignment prescribes the step-size rule — stop when the largest absolute element of the step falls below tol — so that is what this key uses, and it is what the maximization notes use.
Worth knowing for later, though not asked for here: of the three candidates, the score is the most principled, because the maximum is defined by the derivative being zero, while “the step got small” and “the log-likelihood stopped moving” are statements about how the algorithm is behaving rather than about where we are. On a well-conditioned, globally concave problem like this one all three fire within an iteration of each other. On a badly scaled likelihood the step can go small because the curvature is enormous rather than because we have arrived, and there the difference starts to matter.

6. Testing the log-likelihood
At \(\beta = \mathbf{0}\) every observation contributes \(\ln(0.5)\), one or zero alike, so
\[
\ell(\mathbf{0}) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \ln(0.5) = n\ln(0.5).
\]


code
tibble(quantity = c("logit_ll at beta = 0", "n * log(0.5)"),
       value    = c(logit_ll(b_zero, X, sim$y), n * log(0.5)))

title: Exercise #2 — Write the Maximizer (Answers)
text:
7. Testing the score
The score is \(X'(y - \pi)\), and at \(\beta = \mathbf{0}\) that is \(X'(y - 0.5)\). Element by element: the intercept column is all ones, so its entry is \(\sum_i y_i - n/2\); a covariate column \(x_j\) gives \(\sum_i x_{ij}(y_i - 0.5)\).


code
by_hand <- c(sum(sim$y) - n / 2,
             sum(sim$x1 * (sim$y - 0.5)),
             sum(sim$x2 * (sim$y - 0.5)))

tibble(term       = colnames(X),
       from_fn    = logit_score(b_zero, X, sim$y),
       by_hand    = by_hand,
       difference = logit_score(b_zero, X, sim$y) - by_hand)


# A tibble: 3 x 4
  term        from_fn by_hand difference
  <chr>         <dbl>   <dbl>      <dbl>
1 (Intercept)   -401    -401           0
2 x1             267.    267.          0
3 x2            -288    -288           0


Element by element, not as a total. A score can be right in two places and wrong in the third, and a sum would hide it: flip the sign on the x1 element and this table shows x1 off by twice its own value while the intercept and x2 still agree to the last decimal.

title: Exercise #2 — Write the Maximizer (Answers)
text:
8. Testing the Hessian
At \(\beta = \mathbf{0}\) every weight \(\pi_i(1-\pi_i)\) is \(0.5 \times 0.5 = 0.25\). A constant factors out of the matrix product, so the whole Hessian is
\[
H(\mathbf{0}) \;=\; -0.25\,X'X.
\]


code
H_fn   <- logit_hessian(b_zero, X, sim$y)
H_hand <- -0.25 * t(X) %*% X

c(matrices_agree      = isTRUE(all.equal(unname(H_fn), unname(H_hand))),
  intercept_is_neg_qn = isTRUE(all.equal(unname(H_fn[1, 1]), -0.25 * n)),
  diagonal_negative   = all(diag(H_fn) < 0))


     matrices_agree intercept_is_neg_qn   diagonal_negative 
               TRUE                TRUE                TRUE 




code
round(H_fn, 3)


            (Intercept)       x1       x2
(Intercept)     -500.00   -0.680 -248.500
x1                -0.68 -509.209    8.649
x2              -248.50    8.649 -248.500


The intercept’s own diagonal entry is \(-0.25n = -500\), because the intercept column is all ones and \(X'X\) counts the sample.
Why the diagonal has to be negative. A maximum curves downward. The diagonal entry for \(\beta_j\) is how fast the slope in the \(\beta_j\) direction is falling as \(\beta_j\) increases; at a peak it must be falling, so the entry is negative. The standard errors come from inverting \(-H\), and \(-H\) has a positive diagonal only if \(H\) has a negative one. A positive entry in \(H\) would give a negative variance and sqrt() would hand back NaN — which is what separation looks like from inside the algorithm.

9. Testing the whole estimator

3 x2          -1    -0.9009602 -0.9009602 -3.560818e-12           0.9330644

       hand_se      = fit_sim$se,
       glm_se       = sqrt(diag(vcov(m_glm))),
       difference   = fit_sim$se - sqrt(diag(vcov(m_glm))))


# A tibble: 3 x 4
  term           hand_se     glm_se  difference
  <chr>            <dbl>      <dbl>       <dbl>
1 (Intercept) 0.06876222 0.06876219 2.638044e-8
2 x1          0.05694676 0.05694670 6.151835e-8
3 x2          0.1061447  0.1061446  7.054059e-8


Against glm: the coefficients agree to about twelve decimal places and the standard errors to about seven. That is what a correct implementation looks like, and the exact Hessian is why the agreement is this tight — a general-purpose optimizer working from an approximated Hessian does not get this close.
Against the truth: the three ratios are -0.49, -0.86, 0.93 — all comfortably inside one standard error. That is the right comparison and the right result. They will never agree to five decimals, because \(\hat\beta\) is computed from 2,000 draws and the truth is not.
What size gap should worry you. If the estimator is correct each ratio is approximately standard normal, and since we react to the largest of \(k\) of them, the relevant probability is \(1 - (1-p)^k\). With three coefficients: \(\lvert z \rvert\) over 2 turns up in about one run in eight, over 3 in one in 124, over 4 in one in 5,300, and over 6 in one in 170 million.
Two different answers hide in that column, and full credit needs only the first. At 3, go look — not because it is proof, but because the decision is lopsided: checking working code costs ten minutes, and not checking broken code costs a reported result. At 6, luck is off the list; the explanation is in the code.
The better answer, and the one worth rewarding when a student finds it: re-run with a different seed. Sampling noise moves; a bug sits still. Eight runs of the correct estimator here give max \(\lvert z \rvert\) between 0.77 and 1.72 — never near 2. A student who proposes this has understood that the ratio is a statement about repeated samples, which is the whole point of the question.
The distinction students should take away: this is the arithmetic of a \(z\) statistic put to a different use. We are not testing a claim about the world, because we know \(\beta\) — we chose it. The hypothesis on trial is that the code is right.


code
fit_sim$history %>%
  mutate(loglik   = round(loglik, 4),
         max_grad = signif(max_grad, 4),
         max_step = signif(max_step, 4))


# A tibble: 6 x 4
   iter    loglik     max_grad     max_step
  <dbl>     <dbl>        <dbl>        <dbl>
1     1 -1386.294 4.01    e+ 2 6.727   e- 1
2     2 -1106.335 5.163   e+ 1 2.022   e- 1
3     3 -1095.908 5.414   e+ 0 2.56    e- 2
4     4 -1095.779 7.77    e- 2 3.743   e- 4
5     5 -1095.779 1.66    e- 5 7.951   e- 8
6     6 -1095.779 7.198000e-13 3.725000e-15


The log-likelihood climbs fast and then stops moving — nearly all of the gain is in the first two or three steps. The score falls toward zero, and it is the score, not the log-likelihood, that tells you how close you are: the log-likelihood looks converged several iterations before the gradient does, because near the top the surface is flat and large moves in \(\beta\) buy almost no height.

title: Codebook — ces.csv
text:
ces.csv holds 61,000 respondents from the 2020 Cooperative Election Study common content, one row per respondent, subset to twenty columns. Everything except age and the row index arrives as a character string, so nothing is ordered, coded, or labeled for you.
Two general cautions before the variable list. The extract carries no survey weights — the CES commonweight is not among these columns — so anything you compute here is an unweighted sample statistic, not an estimate of the 2020 electorate. And on the policy items, the labels tell you which side a respondent took, not what the side means: on three of them “Support” is the conservative answer and on three others it is the liberal one. The direction column below is the part of this document to read twice.

title: Prediction Methods for MLE Models
Prediction Methods for MLE Models
Prediction Methods for MLE Models
text:
Average effects
Average effects are in-sample, but they build a counterfactual for the variable of interest — they ask what the predictions would look like if the entire sample took a particular value on that variable, while everything else stayed as it is in the data.
Suppose a model of wages with covariates for education and gender. We might ask: what would the predictions look like if the entire sample were male, but otherwise looked as it does? And then: what if the entire sample were female, all else the same? To answer, we set the gender variable to male, generate the prediction for every case, and average; then repeat with gender set to female. The recipe:

estimate the model;
in the estimation data, set the variable of interest to a particular value for the entire sample;
generate the quantities of interest (expected values and standard errors);
take the average, and save it;
repeat for every value of the variable of interest, and plot.

Average effects are often the better choice because they represent the data more completely than a single central-tendency case can.
In symbols, the average effect at a value \(x^{*}\) is
\[
\bar P(x^{*}) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} F(\mathbf{x}_i\widehat\beta),\qquad \text{with every case's } x \text{ of interest set to } x^{*},
\]
where \(\mathbf{x}_i\) is a real row of the estimation sample with only its \(x\) of interest overwritten. So we compute \(n\) predictions, one per case, and average them; then move \(x^{*}\) and do it again. The two approaches differ in what they hold constant. At-means holds the other covariates at one constructed value; average effects hold them at their observed values, all \(n\) of them. And they differ in what they produce: at-means yields one prediction per value of \(x\); average effects yield \(n\) predictions per value, collapsed to their mean.
Put differently, the at-means curve is one case; the average-effects curve is the whole sample. In the linear model, with every covariate held at its mean, these are the same number — the average of the linear predictions is the linear prediction at the averages. Through a nonlinear link they are not: the average of \(F(\cdot)\) across cases is not \(F(\cdot)\) at the average case. We will see the gap between them on the running model below.
