The prediction line over time is flat, and it is flat by construction. Time since the last dispute is not in the model, so it cannot matter: by exclusion, \(\widehat{\beta}\) on time is fixed at zero. A dyad two years past a dispute and a dyad twenty-two years past one are treated as identical observations differing only in \(X\).
Notice this is a choice we made in specifying the model. We assumed \(y_t\) has no bearing on \(y_{t+1}\) — no persistence, no memory from period to period. The rest of this lecture is about a class of models built to ask the question that assumption rules out: how does having survived until now affect the chances of failing now?






Where this connects to last week



The democratic peace data are panel data — cross-sections observed over time — and last week that structure caused us trouble. When we added dyad fixed effects, 621 of 827 dyads turned out never to experience a dispute, and every one of them was perfectly predicted by its own dummy. We treated that as a pathology, which it was. But it is also a description of the data: for most dyads, \(y\) is a long string of zeros occasionally punctuated by a one. That structure is part of why it seems important to think about “memory” or “persistence” over time.

title: Discrete-Time Hazards
section: Two ways to think about time
text:
Two ways to think about time
This invites us to think about how long the spell is a unit survives before it fails.
What do data on spells look like? There are two basic forms.
Survival:
\[\text{Age} = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, \ldots, 87, 88, 89\]
and failure:
\[\text{Death} = 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, \ldots, 0, 0, 1\]
These carry the two halves of the hazard — how many periods the unit survives, and the period in which it fails. They also correspond to the two families of hazard model. To keep them straight, ask yourself what one row of your data is, and what the dependent variable on that row measures.
Continuous-time models: one row per spell, and \(y\) is the survival time. The leader is the row, and the \(y\) variable is “held office for eleven years.” That is the first vector above. We’ll cover continuous-time models in November.
Discrete-time models: one row per period, and \(y\) is the failure indicator. The leader-year is the row, and the \(y\) variable is “did this leader leave office during this year — yes or no.” That is the second vector, and because \(y\) is binary we can estimate it with a binomial log-likelihood, which is to say with a logit.
So the same eleven-year tenure is one row in one setup and eleven rows in the other. That is a reshaping of the same facts, not two different studies, and the section on BTSCS data below is about how to do the reshaping.

The process is continuous; the measurement is not
Here is the distinction - it’s easy to confuse the two. Leaders do not leave office on the first of January. A leader can fall at any hour of any day, and a dispute can start on a Tuesday afternoon — the process runs in continuous time. But Archigos writes down a year, and Oneal and Russett write down a year, so what we get to observe is an interval. The process is continuous and the record is chunked.
Which means the choice between the two families is usually not a choice about the world. It is a choice about the data you were handed. If the record gives you exact dates, you can use them; if it gives you years, you have interval data whether you like it or not, and pretending otherwise does not make the information appear.
Two things follow.
Wide intervals matter more when a lot happens inside them. If the chance of failing in a period is small, it barely matters that we cannot see where in the period the failure fell. If the chance is large, it matters more. Our two datasets sit on either side of this: the annual chance of a dispute is about 4.5%, while the annual chance of a leader losing office is about 19% — four times higher.
Chunked measurement produces ties, in bulk. Because tenure is recorded in whole years, survival time takes very few distinct values, and enormous numbers of leaders share each one. In these data 2,996 exits are spread over just 46 distinct survival times — 65 leaders to a value on average, and 710 of them leaving in their very first year. For a continuous-time model, these “ties” are a nuisance to be worked around, and in November we will see the approximations people use to do it. For a discrete-time model it is not a problem at all: grouped failures are what the model assumes in the first place. When the data come to you in years, the discrete-time model is the one that takes them at face value.






An aside on naming



Models like these are called hazard models, survival models, duration models, or event-history models more or less interchangeably. They all mean modeling the time until an event. The names sometimes signal which quantity is in view: the hazard is the probability of failure at \(t\); survival is the probability of lasting past \(t\). They are opposites. “Event history” usually signals discrete time.

title: Discrete-Time Hazards
section: The same recipe on the dispute data
text:
The same recipe on the dispute data
The leader data are the simple case: a leader takes office once, leaves once, and the spell is over. Dyads are not like that. The United States and Russia can have a dispute, settle, stay quiet for years, and have another one — and in these data they do that repeatedly. Two things change before we run the recipe again.
Units fail more than once, so the clock restarts. We do not follow a dyad across the whole window as a single spell. Every dispute ends a spell, and the year after it begins a new one with the counter back at the start. That is what the cumsum() in the survival-time code was doing. The 827 dyads here generate 1,735 spells; 203 dyads contribute more than one, and the US–Russia dyad alone contributes 33 — its clock restarts 32 times. So the risk set at \(t\) counts spells that reached \(t\), not dyads. The leader data do the same thing in a less obvious way: a leader who returns to office gets a new Archigos id, and the clock starts over.
The counter starts at 0, not 1. Worth spelling out, since the two data sets now sit next to each other in figures.

Why leaders start at 1 and disputes start at 0
The two counters measure different things.

The leader counter is time in office, counting the current year. A leader’s first year is year 1. There is no year 0, because every leader in the data occupies a first year — the clock starts when they take office, and taking office is not a failure.
The dyad counter is years of peace already banked before the current one — Beck, Katz, and Tucker (1998)’s “peace years.” The clock here is started by a failure, and the year immediately after a dispute has no full year of peace behind it. So it is 0. At \(t=1\) one year of peace has elapsed, at \(t=2\) two, and so on.

Two consequences. First, a clock that gets restarted by failures needs a value meaning “just failed,” and that value is 0. It is also where most of the failures are: 593 of the 1,735 spells fail at \(t=0\). Second, every dyad’s first observed year is coded 0 too. The code sets lag(dispute, default = 1), which treats the start of the window as though a dispute had just happened. We cannot see before 1951, so we assume the clock was just reset. That is an assumption, not a measurement, and it is worth knowing it is there.
The offset does not change the model. A cubic in \(t\) is also a cubic in \(t+1\) — shifting the origin is absorbed by the polynomial’s coefficients, and the fit is identical. What it changes is how you read the numbers: “the hazard at \(t=1\)” means a leader’s first year in office, but a dyad’s second year of peace.






Important point



All of this rests on knowing our data extremely well, and on telling the software exactly what we know. R cannot intuit what these rows mean. It cannot tell that obsid is a spell while leadid is a person, that the counter restarts after every dispute but never after a leader takes office, that a zero on the last row of a spell is a censored case rather than a survival, or that one dyad contributes 33 spells. We have to say all of it: what the unit is, what time is counted from, what counts as a failure, whether units can fail more than once, and which spells are censored.
That is both the power of these models and the burden of using them. The power is that the structure carries real information — the risk set, the censoring, the restarting clock — and the model puts it to work. The burden is that we supply the structure by hand and nothing checks us. Get it wrong and the estimates still come back, with standard errors, looking perfectly reasonable. When the data structure is not specified carefully, these models lose their meaning fast.




Doing the counting
Nothing about the recipe changes; only two names do. Group by stime instead of t, and sum dispute instead of leftoffice:

  group_by(t = stime) %>%
  summarise(at_risk = n(), failures = sum(dispute), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(h = failures / at_risk,
         one_minus_h = 1 - h,
         S = cumprod(one_minus_h))

emp_dp %>%
  head(6) %>%
  mutate(across(h:S, ~ round(.x, 3))) %>%
  kbl(caption = "The same counting on the dispute data. Dyad spells, first six years of peace.") %>%
  kable_styling("striped", full_width = FALSE, font_size = 16)

It is \(593/1735 = 0.342\) in the year right after a dispute and \(64/1120 = 0.057\) the year after that — barely a sixth the size, in a single step — then it grinds down under 0.02 and stays there. Disputes beget disputes, and the danger passes quickly. The risk set drains here too, from 1,735 spells to 275, so the same warning applies at the right edge of any figure built on it.
One recipe, two data sets, and two baseline hazards that look nothing alike: collapsing for dyads, high and wandering for leaders. Any model we write has to be flexible enough to produce both.

title: Discrete-Time Hazards
text:
The baseline hazards
The baseline hazards are approximately the constant-only models - they include just the constant and the survival time indicators. The first panel is literally constant only; the second includes survival time; the third includes survival time and its polynomials.


code
grid <- tibble(stime = 0:34) %>%
  mutate(stime2 = stime^2, stime3 = stime^3,
         border = 0, deml = median(survivaldp$deml),
         lncaprat = median(survivaldp$lncaprat), ally = 0)

haz <- function(m, lab) {
  p <- predict(m, newdata = grid, type = "link", se.fit = TRUE)
  tibble(model = lab, stime = grid$stime,
         h  = plogis(p$fit),
         lb = plogis(p$fit - 1.96 * p$se.fit),
         ub = plogis(p$fit + 1.96 * p$se.fit))
}

bind_rows(haz(h_const, "constant"), haz(h_mono, "monotonic"), haz(h_full, "cubic + X")) %>%
  mutate(model = factor(model, levels = c("constant", "monotonic", "cubic + X"))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(stime, h)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lb, ymax = ub), fill = bu_greyfill, alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_line(color = bu_green, linewidth = 0.9) +
  facet_wrap(~ model) +
  labs(title = "Three baseline hazards, Democratic Peace dispute data",
       subtitle = "Letting the baseline vary changes what the model says about time.",
       x = "Years since the last dispute", y = "h(t): Pr(dispute | survived to t)") +
  theme_bu()








Figure 8





The cubic hazard starts at about 0.25 in the year right after a dispute, falls to 0.14 by the next year and 0.02 by year five, bottoms out near 0.007 around year ten, and drifts back up slightly after that. That shape is what the model is telling us: disputes beget disputes, and the risk decays fast. A model without time reports a flat 4% for all of it, which is close to right on average and wrong nearly everywhere.

title: Discrete-Time Hazards
text:
Comparing hazards: Leaders and Disputes


code
dp_shape <- tibble(stime = 0:25) %>%
  mutate(stime2 = stime^2, stime3 = stime^3, border = 0,
         deml = median(survivaldp$deml), lncaprat = median(survivaldp$lncaprat), ally = 0) %>%
  mutate(h = plogis(predict(h_full, newdata = .)), data = "Dyads: time to next dispute")

lt_shape <- map_dfr(1:25, function(tt) {
  d <- lt %>% mutate(t = tt, t2 = tt^2, t3 = tt^3)
  tibble(stime = tt, h = mean(predict(l_cubic, newdata = d, type = "response")))
}) %>% mutate(data = "Leaders: time to leaving office")

bind_rows(dp_shape %>% dplyr::select(stime, h, data), lt_shape) %>%
  ggplot(aes(stime, h)) +
  geom_line(color = bu_green, linewidth = 0.9) +
  facet_wrap(~ data, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(title = "The same model, two different baselines",
       subtitle = "Both are cubic in survival time; the data decide the shape.",
       x = "Survival time", y = "h(t)") +
  theme_bu()








Figure 10





Both hazards fall, and the way they fall is completely different. The dyad hazard collapses: a quarter in the year after a dispute, 2% by year five, and 0.7% by year ten — a thirty-seventh of where it started. The leader hazard decays gently and stays substantial: 0.22 in the first year, 0.19 at five, 0.16 at ten, still 0.08 at twenty-five. Roughly a third of its starting value after a quarter century, where the dyads got there inside three years.
That difference is substantive. A dispute is a shock that fades — having survived a few years of peace, a dyad is nearly out of danger, and the risk is concentrated right after the last fight. Holding office is not like that. Every year in power carries a real chance of losing it, and surviving a decade buys you a lower risk but nothing like safety.
The polynomial does not impose either shape; it permits both. We’ve relaxed the assumption the models are memoryless, or that the baseline hazard is constant. By doing so, we’ve relaxed the assumption that the effects of the \(X\) variables do not change over time. The models and predictions here show both assumptions are wrong and pretty consequential.

title: Discrete-Time Hazards
section: Do estimated hazards match the data?
text:
Do estimated hazards match the data?
We now have a fitted baseline for each dataset, and from earlier we have the raw hazard each is trying to describe. Put them on the same axes. The bars are failures / at risk, straight from the data; the line is the model’s average fitted hazard at each survival time.


code
emp <- bind_rows(emp_dp %>% mutate(data = "Dyads"),
                 emp_lt %>% mutate(data = "Leaders")) %>%
  dplyr::filter(t <= 25)

es_dp <- survivaldp %>% drop_na(dispute, stime, border, deml, lncaprat, ally)

fit_dp <- map_dfr(0:25, function(tt) tibble(t = tt, data = "Dyads",
  h = mean(predict(h_full, newdata = mutate(es_dp, stime = tt, stime2 = tt^2, stime3 = tt^3),
                   type = "response"))))

fit_lt <- map_dfr(1:25, function(tt) tibble(t = tt, data = "Leaders",
  h = mean(predict(l_cubic, newdata = mutate(lt, t = tt, t2 = tt^2, t3 = tt^3),
                   type = "response"))))

ggplot(emp, aes(t, h)) +
  # raw data in neutral grey, model in BU green: the bars carry data so they
  # need a 3:1 color, but a saturated green bar outweighs the fitted line and
  # inverts the hierarchy the subtitle describes
  geom_col(fill = bu_grey, width = 0.7) +
  geom_line(data = bind_rows(fit_dp, fit_lt), aes(t, h), color = bu_green, linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ data, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(title = "The fitted cubic against the raw hazard",
       subtitle = "Bars: failures over units at risk. Line: the model's average fitted hazard.",
       x = "Survival time (years)", y = "h(t)") +
  theme_bu()








Figure 11





Comparing the estimated hazard to the data directly is a good practice - here’s what we learn:
Where it works. The polynomial tracks the dyads’ collapse well from year one onward, and it gets the leaders’ overall level and gentle decline about right.
Where it does not. Look at year zero in the dispute panel: the raw hazard is 0.34 and the fitted line reaches only 0.23. A smooth cubic cannot turn that sharply — it has to approach the spike from somewhere, and in doing so it flattens it. The leader panel shows the mirror-image problem: the raw series bounces between 0.10 and 0.26 through the middle years, and the cubic runs straight through the middle of the bouncing, reading 0.16 at year ten where the data say 0.10.
Neither of those is scandalous, but both point to parts of the hazard we’re not explaining well. What might this tell us in terms of model specification? In the leaders model, the spikes between years 5-8 could be driven in part by democratic electoral cycles; we didn’t include anything to that effect in the model. In the dispute model, the spike in the first year after a dispute could tell us something about the nature of rivalry, and perhaps we need to measure rival dyads.

title: Discrete-Time Hazards
text:
Polity effects
Look at the Polity row, and then look at the estimate from the pooled model.



model
Polity coefficient




leaving office, any cause
\(+0.039\)


regular exit
\(\mathbf{+0.074}\)


irregular exit
\(\mathbf{-0.073}\)



Equal and opposite, and both estimated precisely (\(z = 15.5\) and \(-8.5\)). Democracy makes a leader much more likely to leave through regular channels and much less likely to be removed by force. Those are two mechanisms pulling in two directions, and the pooled model — which reported \(+0.039\) — is reporting their weighted average. It is not that the pooled estimate is imprecise. It is that there is no single quantity for it to estimate.
The same effect shows up elsewhere in the competing risks estimates. Irregular entry raises the hazard of irregular exit sharply (\(+0.737\), \(z = 7.7\)) and does essentially nothing to regular exit (\(+0.146\), \(p = 0.08\)): leaders who seize power are removed by force, not voted out, and the way they arrived predicts the way they will go. Leader age raises both, but regular exit twice as much (\(+0.020\) against \(+0.010\)) — older leaders retire and die in office more than they are deposed.






What the pooled model was actually estimating



Not “the effect of democracy on losing power.” Something closer to “the effect of democracy on losing power, averaged over a mix of two processes whose composition is itself a function of democracy.” That is not a quantity anyone set out to learn about.

title: Mechanism Paper Assignment
text:
The assignment: During the semester, write three short papers. The goal is to identify a causal mechanism you find interesting, discuss its mechanics, its use in the literature, and then to propose a new place to apply it, or a modification of the mechanism applied in an existing location.
What is a mechanism? For our purposes, a mechanism is a set of rules and incentives that point actors toward some behavior they might not otherwise choose. A syllabus in a class can be thought of as a set of mechanisms working together to get students to do three things they otherwise would not do: show up; pay attention; read. A cumulative exam incentivizes keeping up during the semester. Requiring a topic page for a paper assignment incentivizes starting the paper earlier than would otherwise happen. Pop quizzes incentivize attendance and reading.
Here’s another perhaps less trivial example. 17th century pirate ships needed crew members to be willing to fight hard, not to hold back in fear of injury. If pirates were cautious, they would be less effective at taking ships, and would not develop the reputations pirates needed - those fearsome reputations actually made violence less necessary and pirating somewhat safer. To get the crew to fight, captains often made a practice of providing social benefits including health care to those injured. Instead of throwing incapacitated pirates over the side, they provided social insurance, thereby encouraging others to fight hard knowing that injury did not guarantee death. The result was pirate crews willing to take risks and fight aggressively, success in taking target ships, and reputations as fearsome fighters. Captains who guaranteed social benefits created moral hazard, induced risk-taking behavior that benefited the ship.1
Here’s another, even less trivial example, but also a puzzle. Governments of all types extract revenue from citizens via taxation - the more productive citizens are, the more they collect in taxes (holding the rate constant). So governments need to encourage productivity. Productivity requires investment (rather than consumption) - investment pays off in the future while consumption pays off now. For investment to make sense, citizens have to believe the future is valuable and safe. One way governments might try to encourage investment and persuade them the future is safe is to reassure citizens government will not steal from them - if citizens believe government might “change the deal” and seize assets at any time, citizens will neither save, nor invest - they will consume. How can governments maintain the monopoly on violence, but persuade citizens government won’t use that monopoly on violence to seize everything, thereby encouraging investment, and thereby increasing tax revenue? More succinctly, how can a government powerful enough to protect private property guarantee it won’t confiscate private property?2

title: Interactions in Nonlinear Models
text:
Back in the first week’s slides I mentioned that for a logit coefficient, changing any \(x_k\) shifts the prediction along the CDF, so changing a control variable changes the predicted probability even when the variable you care about sits still — and that we would come back to what Nagler (1994) calls the “inherent” interactivity of these models. Time to revisit the always-present “inherent” interactivity and multiplicative interactions.
Here’s where we’re headed:

In a nonlinear model, the effect of \(x_1\) already depends on \(x_2\), whether or not you asked for it. This is compression, and it is a property of the link function, not of your theory.
A multiplicative term \(\beta_3 x_1 x_2\) does something different. Compression makes the effect of \(x_1\) vary in probability space, in a shape the link dictates. A product term makes it vary in the linear predictor, which is where a conditional hypothesis actually lives.
Because both channels are running at once, three questions follow: should I include the interaction? Is the linear form it imposes right? And which of several possible quantities answers my question?

Social scientists have been arguing about interaction terms in nonlinear models for decades, and have been misinterpreting interactions frequently for just as long. Brambor, Clark, and Golder (2006) is the discipline’s standard on specifying and interpreting the linear case, and everything in it still applies here in the nonlinear setting. Berry, DeMeritt, and Esarey (2010) and Berry, Golder, and Milton (2012) argue we can sometimes evaluate conditional claims relying on compression rather than interactions, though Rainey (2016) disagrees, arguing for the interaction term. Hainmueller, Mummolo, and Xu (2019) is about whether the product term you wrote down describes your data. Zhirnov, Moral, and Sedashov (2023) is about which quantity you should have been reporting all along.
Everything you already know about multiplicative interactions in the linear model still holds. If that material is distant in your memory, please review the 501 slides on interactions before going further — I am going to assume you know this material.

title: Interactions in Nonlinear Models
section: Compression: the model is already “inherently” interactive
text:
Compression: the model is already “inherently” interactive
In the logit,
\[
Pr(y=1 \mid x) = \Lambda(x\beta) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-x\beta}},
\]
and the marginal effect of \(x_1\) is not \(\beta_1\). Differentiating through the link,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial Pr(y=1)}{\partial x_1} &= \frac{\partial \Lambda(x\beta)}{\partial (x\beta)} \cdot \frac{\partial (x\beta)}{\partial x_1} \\[4pt]
&= \lambda(x\beta)\,\beta_1 \\[4pt]
&= \Lambda(x\beta)\big(1 - \Lambda(x\beta)\big)\,\beta_1 .
\end{aligned}
\]
Look closely at the last line. The effect of \(x_1\) on the probability is the coefficient \(\beta_1\) times a weight, and the weight is the logistic density evaluated at the linear predictor, \(x\beta\). Generically, for any link whose CDF is \(F\) with density \(f\), the marginal effect is
\[
\frac{\partial Pr(y=1)}{\partial x_1} = f(x\beta)\,\beta_1 ,
\]
and it is the density \(f\) that does the weighting. The logit is the case where that density has a tidy closed form in terms of its own CDF,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\lambda(x\beta) &= \Lambda(x\beta)\big(1 - \Lambda(x\beta)\big) \\
&= p\big(1 - p\big),
\end{aligned}
\]
which is why you see \(p(1-p)\widehat\beta_1\) everywhere. Do not carry that form to other links: the probit’s weight is \(\phi(x\beta)\), and \(\phi(0) = 0.399\), not \(\Phi(0)(1-\Phi(0)) = 0.25\).
So \(\beta_1\) is weighted by the height of the density at \(x\beta\) — not by an area under it. (An area under the density is what you get for a discrete change in \(x\), and we come to that below.)
Let’s think explicitly about what’s in \(x\beta\). Everything. \(x_2\) is in there, and \(x_3\), and the constant. So the weight — and therefore the effect of \(x_1\) — depends on the values of every other variable in the model. Move \(x_2\), and you have changed the weight and so moved the effect of \(x_1\) — in this specific sense, the effect of \(x_1\) depends on the values of the other variables, and so the model is interactive.
This is compression. The term is from Berry, DeMeritt, and Esarey (2010), and it describes what the weight does: as \(x\beta\) moves away from zero and the predicted probability heads toward 0 or 1, the weight shrinks, so the same coefficient buys less and less probability. Effects get compressed against the floor and the ceiling. Nagler (1994) makes the same observation from the other direction, describing these models as “‘interactive’ in all of their variables” with the interactivity inherent in the specification rather than chosen by the analyst (Nagler 1994, 1991; Ai and Norton 2003; Berry, DeMeritt, and Esarey 2010).
Let’s look at the weight.


code
m0 <- glm(dispute ~ border + deml + lncaprat + ally,
          family = binomial(link = "logit"), data = dp)

xb_obs <- predict(m0, type = "link")          # observed linear predictions
grid   <- tibble(xb = seq(-8, 4, 0.02)) %>%
  mutate(lambda = plogis(xb) * (1 - plogis(xb)),
         pr     = plogis(xb))

ggplot(grid, aes(x = xb)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = min(xb_obs), xmax = max(xb_obs),
           ymin = 0, ymax = 0.26, fill = bu_palegreen, alpha = 0.55) +
  geom_line(aes(y = lambda), color = bu_green, linewidth = 1) +
  annotate("segment", x = 0, xend = 0, y = 0, yend = 0.25,
           linetype = "dashed", color = bu_grey) +
  annotate("text", x = 1.3, y = 0.243, hjust = 0, size = 3.6, color = bu_black,
           label = "max weight 0.25, at xb = 0") +
  annotate("text", x = mean(range(xb_obs)), y = 0.13, size = 3.6, color = bu_black,
           label = "range of xb in the\ndemocratic peace model") +
  labs(x = expression(x*beta), y = expression(lambda(x*beta))) +
  theme_bu()








Figure 2: The logistic weight \(\lambda(x\beta) = \Lambda(1-\Lambda)\), with the observed range of the linear predictor in the democratic peace model marked. The weight peaks at 0.25 where \(x\beta = 0\), and the democratic peace data sit almost entirely to the left of that peak.





The weight is largest — exactly \(0.25\) — at \(x\beta = 0\), where the predicted probability is one half, and it falls away symmetrically in both directions. Disputes are rare in these data, so the model lives out on the left tail where the weight is small. And notice what that means: the weight varies by a factor of several across the observed range, so the same \(\beta_1\) produces meaningfully different effects for different cases, entirely because those cases differ on the other covariates.






Important concept



Compression means the nonlinear model is interactive in all of its variables by construction. You do not have to specify anything to get it, and you cannot turn it off. It is a consequence of using a link function that flattens toward 0 and 1.

title: Interactions in Nonlinear Models
text:
Mapping onto the CDF
Let’s reduce the model to two variables — a continuous \(x_1\) you care about and a dummy control \(d\):
\[
Pr(y = 1) = \Lambda(\beta_1 x_1 + \beta_d d).
\]
Figure 3 below shows predictions from this model, so the linear predictor, \(x\beta\) mapped onto the probability space. The horizontal axis is the linear predictor; for a \(d = 0\) case, the effecet is just \(\beta_1 x_1\) — so moving right along the axis means a larger value of the variable of interest. The two CDFs are at the two values of the dummy variable.
Call the dummy’s coefficient \(\beta_d = \delta\), and set it to \(1\) for this figure — an ordinary size for a logit coefficient. The dummy adds \(\delta\) to the linear predictor, which is an intercept shift. Just like the linear model, dummy variables are differential intercepts added to the value of \(\widehat{\beta_0}\). But in the binomial model, we care about the probability, and the probability is the CDF evaluated at \(x\beta\) — so shifting \(x\beta\) slides you along the curve, and how much probability you pick up by sliding depends on how steep the curve is at any given point.


code
delta <- 1     # the dummy's coefficient, on the linear-predictor scale

g <- tibble(xb = seq(-6, 6, 0.01)) %>%
  mutate(`d = 0` = plogis(xb),
         `d = 1` = plogis(xb + delta),
         gap     = `d = 1` - `d = 0`)      # vertical distance between the curves

g_long <- g %>% pivot_longer(c(`d = 0`, `d = 1`),
                             names_to = "grp", values_to = "pr")

# four places to measure the vertical distance between the curves
marks <- tibble(xb = c(-4, -2, 0, 2)) %>%
  mutate(lo = plogis(xb), hi = plogis(xb + delta), gap = hi - lo)

p_curves <- ggplot(g_long, aes(x = xb, y = pr, color = grp, linetype = grp)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_segment(data = marks, aes(x = xb, xend = xb, y = lo, yend = hi),
               inherit.aes = FALSE, color = bu_black, linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_point(data = marks, aes(x = xb, y = lo), inherit.aes = FALSE,
             color = bu_black, size = 1.2) +
  geom_point(data = marks, aes(x = xb, y = hi), inherit.aes = FALSE,
             color = bu_black, size = 1.2) +
  geom_text(data = marks, aes(x = xb + 0.22, y = (lo + hi) / 2,
                              label = sprintf("%.3f", gap)),
            inherit.aes = FALSE, hjust = 0, size = 3.2, color = bu_black) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("d = 0" = bu_green, "d = 1" = bu_lightgreen),
                     name = NULL) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = bu_two_lty, name = NULL) +
  labs(x = expression(x*beta~"for the"~d==0~"group"), y = "Pr(y = 1)",
       color = NULL, linetype = NULL) +
  theme_bu() +
  theme(legend.position = "inside", legend.position.inside = c(0.14, 0.86),
        legend.background = element_blank())

p_gap <- ggplot(g, aes(x = xb, y = gap)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = -delta / 2, color = bu_grey, linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_line(color = bu_green, linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(data = marks, aes(x = xb, y = gap), color = bu_black, size = 1.3) +
  geom_text(data = marks, aes(x = xb, y = gap + 0.016,
                              label = sprintf("%.3f", gap)),
            size = 3.2, color = bu_black) +
  annotate("text", x = -1.9, y = 0.215, hjust = 1, size = 3.1, color = bu_black,
           label = "peak at -delta/2,\nnot at 0") +
  labs(x = expression(x*beta~"for the"~d==0~"group"),
       y = expression(Pr(y==1~"|"~d==1) - Pr(y==1~"|"~d==0))) +
  theme_bu()

p_curves | p_gap








Figure 3: One dummy control on the logistic curve, with no data behind it. Left: both groups lie on the same curve, the \(d=1\) group shifted by \(\delta = 1\), and the four vertical segments are the effect of the dummy. Right: that same vertical distance at every value of \(x\beta\).





Look at the left panel of Figure 3. The two CDFs are the same curve, one slid horizontally by \(\delta\). The four vertical segments measure the effect of being in the \(d=1\) group rather than the \(d=0\) group, and they are all different: \(0.029\) out in the left tail, \(0.150\) partway up, \(0.231\) at the middle, back down to \(0.072\) on the way to the ceiling. Same \(\delta\) every time. Different effect every time.
The right panel is the same quantity at every position rather than at four of them — the vertical distance between the two curves, written \(Pr(y=1 \mid d=1) - Pr(y=1 \mid d=0)\), which is all the \(y\)-axis there means. The four points on it are the four segments from the left panel. And remember what the horizontal axis is: cases further right have a larger \(x_1\). So shifting the value of the control variable changes the effect of \(x_1\), magnifying to varying degrees across the range of \(x\beta\).
A very important note here: the CDF on the left of Figure 3 shows the predicted probability of \(y\) for the cases where \(x_2=0\) and where \(x_2=1\) over the values of \(x_1\). The distances between the two CDFs (.029, .15, .231, etc.) are the differences in the probability of \(y\) given a change in \(x\beta\). In the case of a dummy variable change, these are the marginal effects of \(x_d\) on \(Pr(y=1)\) across the values of \(x_1\). This is an important quantity of interest we’ll use in examining interaction effects.

title: Interactions in Nonlinear Models
section: Is the gap between the two CDFs the density?
text:
Is the gap between the two CDFs the density?
Not quite. The vertical distance between the two curves is
\[
\Lambda(x\beta + \delta) - \Lambda(x\beta) = \int_{x\beta}^{x\beta + \delta} \lambda(u)\,du ,
\]
which is just what a CDF is — a difference of two CDFs is the density accumulated between them. So the gap is an area under the density rather than a height on it, and the width of that area is \(\delta\) itself: a bigger coefficient means a wider strip and so a larger effect.


code
# one strip per mark, running from xb to xb + delta: the interval the dummy moves
# a case across, so the strip width IS delta and is not a display choice
strips <- tibble(xb = numeric(0), x = numeric(0), y = numeric(0))

for (i in seq_len(nrow(marks))) {
  left  <- marks$xb[i]                       # this strip starts here
  xs    <- seq(left, left + delta, length.out = 200)   # ... and is delta wide
  strips <- bind_rows(strips,
                      tibble(xb = left, x = xs, y = dlogis(xs)))
}

ggplot(tibble(x = seq(-6, 6, 0.01), y = dlogis(x)), aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_area(data = strips, aes(x = x, y = y, group = xb),
            fill = bu_palegreen, alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_line(color = bu_green, linewidth = 0.9) +
  # sit each label clear of its own strip: the density is highest at whichever
  # end of [xb, xb+delta] is nearest zero, so clear THAT height
  geom_text(data = marks,
            aes(x = xb + delta / 2,
                y = dlogis(pmin(pmax(0, xb), xb + delta)) + 0.022,
                label = sprintf("%.3f", gap)),
            inherit.aes = FALSE, size = 3.2, color = bu_black) +
  annotate("segment", x = -4, xend = -3, y = 0.145, yend = 0.145,
           color = bu_black, linewidth = 0.5,
           arrow = grid::arrow(ends = "both", length = unit(0.05, "in"))) +
  annotate("text", x = -3.5, y = 0.158, size = 3.2, color = bu_black,
           label = "width = delta = 1") +
  labs(x = expression(x*beta~"for the"~d==0~"group"), y = expression(lambda(x*beta))) +
  theme_bu()








Figure 4: The same four numbers as areas. Each shaded strip runs from \(x\beta\) to \(x\beta + \delta\) under the logistic density; its area is the vertical gap at that \(x\beta\) in Figure 3. The strips are all \(\delta\) wide because \(\delta\) is what the dummy adds to the linear predictor.





Imagine a smaller \(\delta\) - so the coefficient on the dummy variable is small; the shaded area in fig-density-area is smaller, and the weight (\(p(1-p)\)) in the marginal effect \(p(1-p)*\beta_i\) is also smaller. But that same area also has different weight depending on whether we evaluate it at \(x\beta=-3\) or \(x\beta=0\).
This is compression, visualized geometrically. Whether a case sits at \(x\beta = -4\) or \(x\beta = 0\) is determined by its other covariates. So the effect of the dummy depends on the other variables in the model — not because we specified an interaction, but because the curve is not a straight line. On a straight line the gap would be \(\delta\) everywhere, which is exactly the linear model’s structural stability. Bend the line and structural stability is gone whether you wanted it gone or not.

title: Interactions in Nonlinear Models
text:
Predicted probabilities
Let’s generate average predicted probabilities across the values of Polity, and for two types of dyads: contiguous and non-contiguous.


code
V <- vcov(m0)
dem_grid <- seq(-10, 10, 0.5)

# ---- PANEL A: average predicted probability, contiguity off and then on ----
grp <- expand_grid(deml = dem_grid, border = c(0, 1))
grp$pr <- NA_real_
grp$se <- NA_real_

for (i in seq_len(nrow(grp))) {

  Xi <- X                                          # counterfactual COPY
  Xi[, "deml"]   <- grp$deml[i]                    # this democracy score, every dyad
  Xi[, "border"] <- grp$border[i]                  # contiguity off (0) or on (1), every dyad
  # lncaprat and ally are NOT set: each dyad keeps its own

  p         <- plogis(as.vector(Xi %*% b))         # n predicted probabilities
  grp$pr[i] <- mean(p)                             # their average
  g         <- colMeans(p * (1 - p) * Xi)          # gradient of the average wrt beta
  grp$se[i] <- sqrt(as.numeric(t(g) %*% V %*% g))
}

grp <- grp %>%
  mutate(grp = factor(border, levels = c(0, 1),
                      labels = c("not contiguous", "contiguous")),
         lo = pr - 1.96 * se, hi = pr + 1.96 * se)

# ---- PANEL B: average marginal effect of contiguity, at each democracy value ----
# border is binary, so its "marginal effect" is the 0 -> 1 discrete change,
# computed for every dyad and then averaged
gapd     <- tibble(deml = dem_grid)
gapd$ame <- NA_real_
gapd$se  <- NA_real_

for (i in seq_along(dem_grid)) {

  X0 <- X                                          # two counterfactual COPIES
  X1 <- X
  X0[, "deml"]   <- dem_grid[i]                    # same democracy score in both
  X1[, "deml"]   <- dem_grid[i]
  X0[, "border"] <- 0                              # nobody contiguous
  X1[, "border"] <- 1                              # everybody contiguous

  p0 <- plogis(as.vector(X0 %*% b))                # n predictions with border = 0
  p1 <- plogis(as.vector(X1 %*% b))                # n predictions with border = 1

  gapd$ame[i] <- mean(p1 - p0)                     # average the n differences
  g           <- colMeans(p1 * (1 - p1) * X1) - colMeans(p0 * (1 - p0) * X0)
  gapd$se[i]  <- sqrt(as.numeric(t(g) %*% V %*% g))
}

gapd <- gapd %>% mutate(lo = ame - 1.96 * se, hi = ame + 1.96 * se)

p_lev <- ggplot(grp, aes(x = deml, y = pr, color = grp, linetype = grp)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(x = deml, ymin = lo, ymax = hi, group = grp),
              inherit.aes = FALSE, fill = bu_palegreen, alpha = 0.45) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("not contiguous" = bu_green,
                                "contiguous" = bu_lightgreen), name = NULL) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = bu_two_lty, name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "A. Average predicted probability",
       x = NULL, y = "Pr(dispute)", color = NULL, linetype = NULL) +
  theme_bu() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 11, face = "bold"),
        legend.position = "inside", legend.position.inside = c(0.79, 0.84),
        legend.background = element_blank(),
        panel.border = element_rect(color = bu_grey, fill = NA, linewidth = 0.3))

p_dif <- ggplot(gapd, aes(x = deml, y = ame)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = bu_palegreen, alpha = 0.45) +
  geom_line(color = bu_green, linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = bu_grey) +
  expand_limits(y = 0) +
  labs(title = "B. Average marginal effect of contiguity (the gap in A)",
       x = "weak-link democracy", y = "change in Pr(dispute)") +
  theme_bu() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 11, face = "bold"),
        panel.border = element_rect(color = bu_grey, fill = NA, linewidth = 0.3))

p_lev / p_dif + plot_layout(heights = c(2, 1.25))








Figure 5: Panel A: average predicted probability of a dispute across weak-link democracy, with contiguity set on and then off for the whole sample. Panel B: the average marginal effect of contiguity — the vertical distance between the two curves in A — at each value of democracy. Bands are 95% delta-method intervals. There is no product term in this model.





Panel A of Figure 5 is the left panel of Figure 3, zoomed way in on the lower-left corner. Disputes are rare, so both groups live down near the floor of the curve, and neither line gets anywhere near the steep middle.
Panel B plots the vertical distance between the two curves in Panel A — the average marginal effect of contiguity, at each value of democracy. Contiguity is binary, so its “marginal effect” is the discrete \(0 \to 1\) change, computed for every dyad in the sample and then averaged; the bands are delta-method intervals on that average. It runs from 0.063 among the most autocratic dyads down to 0.018 among the most democratic, a factor of 3.6, and the interval never comes near zero. So contiguity matters 3.6 times as much for autocracies as for democracies, in a model that contains no interaction of any kind.
This illustrates an important point about inherent interactivity in nonlinear models. Absent an explicit multiplicative interaction, we can still say the effect of democracy on conflict depends on contiguity. That effect is small and slopes gradually downward among non-contiguous states; for contiguous states it is considerably larger and steeper.
We can tell the same story but from another vantage point if we look at Panel B. The average marginal effect of contiguity is positive — contiguity raises the probability of a dispute everywhere - the curve in Panel B sits above zero across the whole range — but it is declining in democracy, which is Panel B’s downward slope. The marginal effect of contiguity is positive, but declines with democracy.

title: Interactions in Nonlinear Models
text:
The value of marginal effects
For nonlinear models, coefficients imply constant effects - take a look at any of the coefficient tables we’ve discussed this semester, and you’ll see things like \(\widehat\beta_{\text{contiguity}} = 1.04\). That single estimate can easily lead us to think this is the estimated effect for any scenario we can construct in the data.
But the discussion above illustrates this is not true. We should spend time exploring and then illustrating to our readers where the effects are larger or smaller as we’ve done in the case of democracy and geographic contiguity. There, we’ve shown that the effect of contiguity is large in exacerbating conflict propensity among non-democratic states. Those states are already more prone to conflict, and sharing a border fans those flames far more than among democratic states that share borders. In other words, the effect of contiguity is not constant.
Marginal effects are a quantity that help us tell that story. The marginal effect of contiguity depends on the value of democracy such that the poisonous effect of shared borders diminishes with increasing democracy.

title: Interactions in Nonlinear Models
section: Testing an interaction, Democracy x Contiguity
text:
Testing an interaction, Democracy x Contiguity
Let’s evaluate a model including the explicit multiplicative interaction between Polity and contiguity, and comparing that model to the model without. In effect, we’re testing compression versus compression plus interaction.


code
m1 <- glm(dispute ~ border * deml + lncaprat + ally,
          family = binomial(link = "logit"), data = dp)

modelsummary(list("No product term" = m0, "With product term" = m1),
             stars = TRUE, gof_map = c("nobs", "logLik", "aic"),
             coef_rename = c("border" = "Contiguous",

Now let’s compare the average marginal effects from the two (but not lose sight of the fact that the interaction model is not a better fit to the data).


code
X1 <- model.matrix(m1)
b1 <- coef(m1)

# same calculation as before, but the product column has to move with border
ame_deml_int <- function(bord) {
  Xi <- X1
  Xi[, "border"]      <- bord
  Xi[, "border:deml"] <- bord * Xi[, "deml"]
  p <- plogis(as.vector(Xi %*% b1))
  mean(p * (1 - p)) * (b1["deml"] + bord * b1["border:deml"])
}

tibble(model = c("no product term", "with product term"),
       ame_border0 = c(ame_deml(0), ame_deml_int(0)),
       ame_border1 = c(ame_deml(1), ame_deml_int(1))) %>%
  mutate(ratio = ame_border1 / ame_border0)


# A tibble: 2 x 4
  model             ame_border0 ame_border1 ratio

1 no product term      -0.00190    -0.00469  2.46
2 with product term    -0.00212    -0.00438  2.06


The model with no product term says democracy’s effect is 2.46 times larger among neighbors. The model with a product term — an insignificant one — says 2.06 times larger. Any conditional effect between democracy and contiguity arises from compression, not from the interaction.






Important point



A null product term does not mean “no interaction.” It means no interaction beyond what the link was already doing via compression. Reporting “I find no interaction effect” after a table like Table 1 is a substantively false statement about this model, which says democracy matters two and a half times as much among neighbors. The model is pretty clearly interactive, just through compression, not through a multiplicative interaction.

title: Interactions in Nonlinear Models
section: Testing the interaction of Democracy x Capabilities
text:
Testing the interaction of Democracy x Capabilities
Let’s examine another interaction in the same data. The substantive question is, surprisingly, one not often asked in the conflict literature: does democracy’s pacifying effect depend on the balance of power between the two states? The two variables are not the same kind of thing, and it matters later. The capability ratio is continuous — 10,636 distinct values in 20,990 rows. Weak-link democracy is a 21-point ordered index: every value from \(-10\) to \(+10\), integers only, and every one of them observed. We enter it as a single linear term, which is what the literature conventionally does and which quietly assumes the 21 steps are evenly spaced in their effect on the log-odds. That is an assumption, not a measurement fact.


code
m2 <- glm(dispute ~ border + deml * lncaprat + ally,
          family = binomial(link = "logit"), data = dp)

modelsummary(list("No product term" = m0, "Democracy x Capabilities" = m2),
             stars = TRUE, gof_map = c("nobs", "logLik", "aic"),
             coef_rename = c("border" = "Contiguous",
                             "deml" = "Weak-link democracy",
                             "lncaprat" = "ln(capability ratio)",
                             "ally" = "Allied",
                             "deml:lncaprat" = "Democracy x ln(cap ratio)"),
             output = "kableExtra")
anova(m0, m2, test = "LRT")

The interaction model fits the data better than the model without: \(\chi^2 = 23.2\) on one degree of freedom, \(p < 0.0001\). So let’s interpret the interaction model, but be cautious about interpreting the coefficients just as we were in the interactive linear model.
The coefficient on democracy is \(-0.1144\). That is not the effect of democracy. It is the effect of democracy when \(\text{lncaprat} = 0\) — that is, in a perfectly matched dyad, where the two states have identical capabilities. That value actually exists in the data (the minimum), so the number is interpretable here. It often is not. The coefficient on the capability ratio, \(-0.1157\), is likewise the effect of the capability ratio among fully autocratic dyads, where \(\text{deml} = -10\)… except that is wrong, and it is wrong in a way worth catching: \(\text{deml} = 0\) is a middling Polity score, not an autocratic one, so that coefficient describes an anocratic dyad. Recognize when your constituent variable has a meaningful zero somewhere odd.

title: Interactions in Nonlinear Models
text:
Describing the interaction
Describing an interaction finding means answering two questions - many folks skip the second one:

How does the effect of democracy change as the power balance changes? The answer is a marginal effect plot.
Do the cases that function describes actually exist? A conditional-effect plot will give you an effect at every value of the moderating variable whether or not any dyads exist there. We need to evaluate where the data actually support predictions.

We will do them in that order, and the second will change the answer to the first. Take question 1 first.

title: Interactions in Nonlinear Models
section: The conditional effect, on the log-odds scale
text:
The conditional effect, on the log-odds scale
The quantity is the effect of democracy as a function of the capability ratio:
\[
\frac{\partial (x\beta)}{\partial \text{deml}} = \widehat\beta_{\text{deml}} + \widehat\beta_{\text{deml} \times \text{cap}} \cdot \text{lncaprat},
\]
Its standard error is the three-term variance from the top of these slides, so let’s write it out for this model and put numbers in it.
Notation first, to keep the display readable: let \(w\) stand for lncaprat, and write \(\widehat\beta_d\) for the democracy coefficient and \(\widehat\beta_{dc}\) for the interaction. The conditional effect is then \(\widehat\beta_d + w\,\widehat\beta_{dc}\); a sum in which one piece is multiplied by a constant — and the variance of such a sum is
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{Var}\big(\widehat\beta_d + w\,\widehat\beta_{dc}\big)
&= \mathrm{Var}(\widehat\beta_d) \\[2pt]
&\quad + w^{2}\,\mathrm{Var}(\widehat\beta_{dc}) \\[2pt]
&\quad + 2w\,\mathrm{Cov}(\widehat\beta_d,\,\widehat\beta_{dc}).
\end{aligned}
\]
That is a variance. What we plot, and what goes in an interval, is its square root:
\[
\mathrm{SE}\big(\widehat\beta_d + w\,\widehat\beta_{dc}\big) =
\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(\widehat\beta_d) + w^{2}\,\mathrm{Var}(\widehat\beta_{dc}) + 2w\,\mathrm{Cov}(\widehat\beta_d,\,\widehat\beta_{dc})} ,
\]
which is the form Brambor, Clark, and Golder (2006) give. Keep the two apart when you read the numbers below: the three terms add up inside the square root, so they are on the variance scale, and only the last column is a standard error.
Why plot the linear predictor and not the probability? To facilitate seeing where the effect is and where the data are. The linear prediction isolates the interaction you specified from the compression that was there anyway. Everything in the first half of these slides said the effect of democracy varies across cases even with no product term. On the probability scale you cannot see which of the two channels is doing the work, because they multiply. In the linear plot, compression is gone — \(\lambda(x\beta)\) has dropped out — and what is left is your product term and nothing else.
So read this plot as a statement about the model and data, not about interpretation. We will put it back on the probability scale later, where it is interpretable but no longer clean.


code
b2 <- coef(m2); V2 <- vcov(m2)
w  <- seq(0, 9, 0.05)

cond <- tibble(lncaprat = w) %>%
  mutate(eff = b2["deml"] + lncaprat * b2["deml:lncaprat"],
         se  = sqrt(V2["deml", "deml"] +
                    lncaprat^2 * V2["deml:lncaprat", "deml:lncaprat"] +
                    2 * lncaprat * V2["deml", "deml:lncaprat"]),
         lo  = eff - 1.96 * se,
         hi  = eff + 1.96 * se)

cross <- -b2["deml"] / b2["deml:lncaprat"]     # where the conditional effect hits zero

p_eff <- ggplot(cond, aes(x = lncaprat, y = eff)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = bu_palegreen, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_line(color = bu_green, linewidth = 1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = bu_grey) +
  annotate("segment", x = cross, xend = cross, y = -0.13, yend = 0,
           linetype = "dotted", color = bu_black) +
  annotate("text", x = cross - 0.1, y = -0.115, hjust = 1, size = 3.6, color = bu_black,
           label = paste0("crosses zero at ", round(cross, 2))) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "effect of democracy on log-odds of dispute") +
  theme_bu()

p_hist <- ggplot(dp, aes(x = lncaprat)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 45, fill = bu_green, color = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = quantile(dp$lncaprat, 0.9), linetype = "dashed", color = bu_black) +
  annotate("text", x = quantile(dp$lncaprat, 0.9) + 0.15, y = Inf, vjust = 1.6,
           hjust = 0, size = 3.4, color = bu_black, label = "90th percentile") +
  labs(x = "ln(capability ratio)", y = "dyad-years") +
  theme_bu()

p_eff / p_hist + plot_layout(heights = c(2.2, 1))








Figure 7: The conditional effect of weak-link democracy on the log-odds of a dispute, across the logged capability ratio, with 95% confidence bands. The histogram underneath shows where the data actually are.





Read Figure 7 from the left. Among evenly matched dyads democracy is strongly pacifying, about \(-0.114\) on the log-odds and tightly estimated. As the power gap widens the pacifying effect shrinks, crosses zero at a logged capability ratio of about 5.98, and turns positive. Read literally, the model says democracy pacifies matched dyads and provokes badly mismatched ones.
That is a real answer to question 1, and if we stopped here we would report it. The standard error is doing its job, the band widens where it should, and the interval excludes zero at both ends.
Which is exactly why question 2 matters. Everything just described is a property of a line; none of it is a claim about the data. Look at the histogram underneath, and notice that the interesting half of the finding — the part where the sign turns positive — sits out where the bars have run out.

title: Interactions in Nonlinear Models
text:
Where the data actually are
Let’s cut the moderator, ln(capabilities) into deciles and count. Each row is a tenth of the sample, so the width of a row’s range tells you how stretched the data are there, and the disputes column tells you what is actually estimating the model.


code
cross_dec <- findInterval(cross, quantile(dp$lncaprat, seq(0, 1, 0.1)),
                          rightmost.closed = TRUE)

dp %>%
  mutate(decile = ntile(lncaprat, 10)) %>%
  group_by(decile) %>%
  summarise(from = min(lncaprat), to = max(lncaprat),
            n = n(), disputes = sum(dispute), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(`ln(cap ratio)` = paste0(sprintf("%.2f", from), " - ", sprintf("%.2f", to)),
         `capability ratio` = paste0(round(exp(from)), ":1 - ", round(exp(to)), ":1"),
         `Pr(dispute)`   = disputes / n,
         note = if_else(decile == cross_dec, "<- effect crosses zero in here", "")) %>%
  dplyr::select(decile, `ln(cap ratio)`, `capability ratio`, n, disputes,
                `Pr(dispute)`, note) %>%
  kbl(digits = c(0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 4, 0),
      col.names = c("decile", "ln(cap ratio)", "capability ratio", "dyad-years",
                    "disputes", "Pr(dispute)", "")) %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE) %>%

Now put Figure 7 next to Table 3. The dotted line in the figure sits at \(\text{lncaprat} = 5.98\), and the bold row of the table is the decile that contains it: the 9th, running from 5.1 to 6.06. That is the 89.5th percentile of the data. Everything to the right of that line — the entire region where this model says democracy provokes conflict — is the top 11% of dyads.
And the effect does not become statistically positive until 8.27, which is inside the last decile, at the 99.8th percentile. The claim rests on the sparsest two-tenths of one percent of the sample.
Look at the last two rows of Table 3 for the reason this is worse than a row count suggests. The top decile alone spans 6.06 to 8.97 — about a third of the moderator’s entire range squeezed into one tenth of the observations — and what estimates a logit is not rows but events. Read the disputes column down: it is the count of ones, and in a rare-outcome model those thin out long before the sample size does.

title: Interactions in Nonlinear Models
text:
What the data say instead
The natural objection is that this is just imprecision, and the widening band already reported it. It is not. The product term is not only extrapolating far, it is extrapolating along a shape we imposed, and that shape can be checked directly.
Hainmueller, Mummolo, and Xu (2019)’s binning estimator does it in four steps, and it is worth being concrete about each one because the regression looks odd the first time you see it.

Cut the moderator into bins. Here, terciles of lncaprat — a low, mid and high third of the dyad-years, roughly 7,000 each.
Refit, letting democracy have its own slope inside every bin. That is what bin:deml does without a deml term of its own in the formula: with no main effect to be a deviation from, R returns one democracy coefficient per bin, each estimated only from the dyads in that bin. We do the same for lncaprat so each bin gets its own capability slope too, and border and ally stay common across bins.
Plot those three coefficients at the median lncaprat of their bin, on top of the straight line the product-term model drew.
Ask whether the three points lie on the line. They are estimates of the same quantity — the effect of democracy at that part of the capability range — computed two ways. The line got there by assuming the effect moves linearly in lncaprat. The points did not assume anything of the kind: each one is free to be whatever the dyads in its bin say.

So this is a test of the functional form, with the bins as the flexible alternative and the line as the restriction. If the assumption is harmless the points scatter around the line; if it is not, they tell you what shape the data actually have.


code
dpb <- dp %>%
  mutate(bin = cut(lncaprat,
                   breaks = quantile(lncaprat, c(0, 1/3, 2/3, 1)),
                   include.lowest = TRUE,
                   labels = c("low", "mid", "high")))

# a separate democracy slope, and a separate capability slope, inside each bin
mbin <- glm(dispute ~ border + ally + bin + bin:deml + bin:lncaprat,
            family = binomial(link = "logit"), data = dpb)

bin_med <- dpb %>% group_by(bin) %>% summarise(med = median(lncaprat), n = n())

bins <- tidy(mbin) %>%
  filter(str_detect(term, ":deml")) %>%
  mutate(bin = str_remove(str_remove(term, ":deml"), "bin")) %>%
  left_join(bin_med, by = "bin") %>%
  mutate(lo = estimate - 1.96 * std.error,
         hi = estimate + 1.96 * std.error)

ggplot(cond, aes(x = lncaprat)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = bu_palegreen, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_line(aes(y = eff), color = bu_green, linewidth = 1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = bu_grey) +
  geom_pointrange(data = bins, aes(x = med, y = estimate, ymin = lo, ymax = hi),
                  color = bu_black, size = 0.5) +
  labs(x = "ln(capability ratio)",
       y = "effect of democracy on log-odds of dispute") +
  theme_bu()








Figure 8: The binning estimator. Points are separately-estimated effects of democracy within terciles of the capability ratio, plotted at the bin medians, against the line the product term implies.







code
bins %>%
  mutate(linear_implied = b2["deml"] + med * b2["deml:lncaprat"]) %>%
  dplyr::select(bin, n, median_lncaprat = med, binned = estimate, lo, hi, linear_implied)


# A tibble: 3 x 7
  bin       n median_lncaprat  binned      lo      hi linear_implied

1 low    7000            1.02 -0.0833 -0.102  -0.0642        -0.0949
2 mid    6993            3.06 -0.0883 -0.113  -0.0642        -0.0559
3 high   6997            5.37  0.0134 -0.0166  0.0435        -0.0116


Read the middle bin first — it is where the disagreement is. The line has to travel from about \(-0.095\) at the low bin’s median to \(-0.012\) at the high bin’s, so it must pass through roughly \(-0.056\) in between. The data in that middle third say \(-0.088\), with an interval of \([-0.113, -0.064]\) — and the line’s value sits outside it. The middle bin is statistically indistinguishable from the low bin (\(-0.083\) against \(-0.088\), a gap of 0.005), where the line says the two should differ by about \(0.04\).
Now notice what the other two bins do, because this is the part that is easy to get backwards. They agree with the line. At the low bin the line says \(-0.095\) and the interval is \([-0.102, -0.064]\), which contains it. At the high bin the line says \(-0.012\) and the interval is \([-0.017, 0.043]\), which also contains it. The high bin’s estimate is not distinguishable from zero — but neither is the line’s prediction there, so that bin is not evidence of anything. A bin that fails to reject is not a bin that disagrees.
So the case rests on the middle third, and it is worth testing rather than eyeballing. Fit the interaction with a linear moderator, then add bin-specific democracy shifts on top, and ask whether those shifts are jointly zero:


code
# restricted: the effect of democracy moves linearly in lncaprat
b_lin <- glm(dispute ~ border + ally + bin + bin:lncaprat + deml + deml:lncaprat,
             family = binomial(link = "logit"), data = dpb)
# flexible: the same, plus a separate democracy shift in each bin
b_flex <- glm(dispute ~ border + ally + bin + bin:lncaprat + deml + deml:lncaprat +
                bin:deml,
              family = binomial(link = "logit"), data = dpb)

anova(b_lin, b_flex, test = "LRT")


Analysis of Deviance Table

Model 1: dispute ~ border + ally + bin + bin:lncaprat + deml + deml:lncaprat
Model 2: dispute ~ border + ally + bin + bin:lncaprat + deml + deml:lncaprat + 
    bin:deml
  Resid. Df Resid. Dev Df Deviance Pr(>Chi)   
1     20980     6954.0                        
2     20978     6941.3  2   12.732 0.001719 **
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


It rejects: \(\chi^2 = 12.73\) on 2 degrees of freedom, \(p = 0.0017\). The linear form is wrong in these data, and the failure is in the middle of the distribution rather than out in the sparse tail.
What shape is it, then? Flat and then falling away: democracy pacifies near-parity and moderately mismatched dyads by about the same amount, and stops mattering among the badly mismatched. And that shape explains where the sign change came from. A straight line forced through a flat-then-drop pattern has to keep descending past the last bin to fit the left-hand part, and descending past zero is what produces “democracy provokes.” The reversal is a property of the line, not a feature the bins ever show.
Be careful about how much the binning proves on its own, though. The high bin averages the effect across everything from a 61:1 capability gap to 7893:1, so “about zero over that whole range” is consistent with an effect that is mildly negative for most of it. What rules the reversal out is the combination: the shape here, the common support from Table 3, and — as we will see below — the fact that on the probability scale the interval never clears zero anywhere.






Important concept



Common support and functional form are the same problem wearing two hats. Common support tells you where the model is speaking without data. The shape you imposed determines what it says there. Checking only the first leaves you saying “the estimate is uncertain at the extreme”; checking both lets you say what the data actually support, which here is a different substantive claim.


So describe it accurately. Democracy’s pacifying effect is about the same among evenly matched and moderately mismatched dyads, and it disappears among badly mismatched ones. Whether it reverses is not something these data can support: the bins never show it, and the region where the line claims it holds a fifth of one percent of the dyads.
Know your data - and make this same demand of the authors you read. When a paper you’re reading shows you a figure like this, think about the underlying data distribution and whether or to what extent those data are likely to support the predictive claims the paper shows you.

title: Interactions in Nonlinear Models
section: Both quantities, on the capability interaction
text:
Both quantities, on the capability interaction
Let’s plot the average predicted probabilities for each value of democracy and setting ln(capabilities) to the three values from the terciles in the binning exercise above. Interacting two continuous variables (or in our case, one continuous and one many-categoried variable) leaves us with too many possible combinations of our interacted variables. The common solution is to choose a finite number of sensible values of one of them. So I’m computing across all of Polity for three values of ln(capabilities).
The three capability ratios are the tercile medians from the binning, translated out of logs so they say something: \(3 : 1\), \(21 : 1\) and \(215 : 1\). These would correspond to dyads near parity, dyads with imbalances, and dyads with extreme imbalances. Confidence bands are delta-method intervals on the average.


code
X2 <- model.matrix(m2)

cr_levels <- c(1.02, 3.06, 5.37)                  # tercile medians of lncaprat
cr_labels <- paste0(round(exp(cr_levels)), " : 1")
dem_grid  <- seq(-10, 10, 0.5)

# one row for every (democracy, capability ratio) pair we want a prediction at
pp     <- expand_grid(deml = dem_grid, cr = cr_levels)
pp$pr  <- NA_real_                                # average predicted probability
pp$se  <- NA_real_                                # its delta-method standard error

for (i in seq_len(nrow(pp))) {

  Xi <- X2                                        # counterfactual COPY of the design matrix
  Xi[, "deml"]          <- pp$deml[i]             # this democracy score, for every dyad
  Xi[, "lncaprat"]      <- pp$cr[i]               # this capability ratio, for every dyad
  Xi[, "deml:lncaprat"] <- pp$deml[i] * pp$cr[i]  # the product column tracks BOTH of them
  # border and ally are deliberately NOT set: each dyad keeps its own

  p        <- plogis(as.vector(Xi %*% b2))        # n predicted probabilities
  pp$pr[i] <- mean(p)                             # their average

  g        <- colMeans(p * (1 - p) * Xi)          # gradient of that average wrt beta
  pp$se[i] <- sqrt(as.numeric(t(g) %*% V2 %*% g))
}

pp <- pp %>%
  mutate(grp = factor(cr, levels = cr_levels, labels = cr_labels),
         lo  = pr - 1.96 * se,
         hi  = pr + 1.96 * se)

# the four corners quoted in the text below, pulled out as plain numbers
pp_par_lo <- pp$pr[pp$deml == -10 & pp$cr == cr_levels[1]]
pp_par_hi <- pp$pr[pp$deml ==  10 & pp$cr == cr_levels[1]]
pp_gap_lo <- pp$pr[pp$deml == -10 & pp$cr == cr_levels[3]]
pp_gap_hi <- pp$pr[pp$deml ==  10 & pp$cr == cr_levels[3]]

ggplot(pp, aes(x = deml, y = pr, color = grp, linetype = grp)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(x = deml, ymin = lo, ymax = hi, group = grp), inherit.aes = FALSE,
              fill = bu_palegreen, alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_color_bu(name = "capability ratio") +
  scale_linetype_bu(name = "capability ratio") +
  labs(x = "weak-link democracy", y = "average Pr(dispute)") +
  theme_bu() +
  theme(legend.position = "inside", legend.position.inside = c(0.78, 0.8),
        legend.background = element_blank())








Figure 9: Average adjusted predictions: the average predicted probability of a dispute if every dyad in the sample had the stated democracy score and capability ratio, with its own contiguity and alliance left as observed. Bands are 95% delta-method intervals.





The figure facilitates describing the conditional effect. Among near-parity dyads (about \(3:1\)), moving from full autocracy to full democracy takes the probability of a dispute from 0.093 to 0.016 — about 7.8 percentage points. Among badly mismatched dyads (about \(215:1\)) the same transition from autocratic to democratic takes it from 0.027 to 0.021, a drop of 0.5 percentage points. Democratization buys roughly 14 times as much peace between equals as between a great power and a weak one.
This is an interesting finding not often represented in the literature. Democratic institutions appear to constrain the use of capabilities even when we disaggregate balanced and imbalanced pairs of states. Non-democratic institutions allow leaders to use capabilities more freely and they appear to do so. The disaggregation indicates that balanced autocrats are considerably more likely to fight than are imbalanced autocrats. Balanced democrats are no more conflict prone than are imbalanced democratic pairs.
Two more things Figure 9 shows that Figure 7 cannot. The curves cross, at about democracy \(=\) 6. That is the interaction read from the other side: the vertical distance between curves is the effect of the capability ratio, and it vanishes right there. An interaction is symmetric, so “democracy’s effect depends on the power balance” and “the power balance’s effect depends on democracy” are one claim — it’s important to consider how you state the interaction hypothesis and what quantities you predict given your theory model.

title: Interactions in Nonlinear Models
text:
Marginal Effects
Let’s turn to marginal effects. Both panels below are average marginal effects — computed once for every dyad in the sample and then averaged, exactly as the predictions above were — and both are on the probability scale. The two below differ only in what counts as “a change in democracy.”
Panel A, the derivative. For each dyad: hold its own contiguity and alliance, set its capability ratio to the value on the horizontal axis, and evaluate \[
\frac{\partial Pr(\text{dispute})}{\partial\,\text{deml}} = \lambda(x_i\beta)\big(\widehat\beta_{\text{deml}} + \widehat\beta_{\text{deml}\times\text{cap}} \cdot \text{lncaprat}\big).
\] Average those 20,990 numbers. Note what is inside: the bracket is the log-odds (linear) conditional effect from Figure 7, and \(\lambda(x_i\beta)\) is the compression weight from the first half of the deck. The probability-scale effect is the two of them multiplied, which is exactly why this figure is not a straight line and Figure 7 is.
Panel B, the discrete difference. For each dyad, predict twice — once with deml set to \(-10\), once at \(+10\), capability ratio set to the axis value both times — subtract, and average the differences. No derivative anywhere; it is the gap between two average adjusted predictions, the same quantity the endpoints of Figure 9 give.
Intervals on both are the delta method, with the gradient taken through whichever of those two calculations produced the estimate.
The tick marks along the bottom of each panel are a rug plot — one short vertical mark per observation, placed at that case’s value on the horizontal axis. It is the cheapest way to put the data underneath a fitted line, and it costs one line of code (geom_rug()). Read it as a flattened histogram: dense black where cases pile up, sparse where they thin out. Here it tells you at a glance that the right-hand third of both panels is drawn over very little data, which is the point the whole previous section had to make with a table.


code
cr_grid <- seq(0, 9, 0.1)          # capability ratios to evaluate at

# ---- PANEL A: average marginal effect of democracy (a derivative) -----------
ame_est <- numeric(length(cr_grid))
ame_se  <- numeric(length(cr_grid))

for (i in seq_along(cr_grid)) {

  Xi <- X2                                              # counterfactual COPY
  Xi[, "lncaprat"]      <- cr_grid[i]                   # this capability ratio, every dyad
  Xi[, "deml:lncaprat"] <- Xi[, "deml"] * cr_grid[i]    # product tracks BOTH columns
  # deml is deliberately NOT set. Every dyad keeps its own democracy score, which
  # is what makes this an AVERAGE marginal effect rather than the effect at some
  # constructed democracy value.

  p     <- plogis(as.vector(Xi %*% b2))                 # n predicted probabilities
  slope <- b2["deml"] + cr_grid[i] * b2["deml:lncaprat"]  # effect on the LOG-ODDS

  ame_est[i] <- mean(p * (1 - p)) * slope               # weight each case, then average

  # delta gradient: the estimate is mean(weight) x slope, and beta moves both
  g <- colMeans(p * (1 - p) * (1 - 2 * p) * Xi) * slope
  g["deml"]          <- g["deml"] + mean(p * (1 - p))
  g["deml:lncaprat"] <- g["deml:lncaprat"] + mean(p * (1 - p)) * cr_grid[i]
  ame_se[i] <- sqrt(as.numeric(t(g) %*% V2 %*% g))
}

# ---- PANEL B: average discrete change, democracy from -10 to +10 -----------
dd_est <- numeric(length(cr_grid))
dd_sd  <- numeric(length(cr_grid))

for (i in seq_along(cr_grid)) {

  Xlo <- X2                                             # two counterfactual COPIES
  Xhi <- X2
  Xlo[, "lncaprat"]      <- cr_grid[i]                  # same capability ratio in both
  Xhi[, "lncaprat"]      <- cr_grid[i]
  Xlo[, "deml"]          <- -10                         # fully autocratic
  Xhi[, "deml"]          <-  10                         # fully democratic
  Xlo[, "deml:lncaprat"] <- -10 * cr_grid[i]            # products track both columns
  Xhi[, "deml:lncaprat"] <-  10 * cr_grid[i]

  plo <- plogis(as.vector(Xlo %*% b2))                  # n predictions at deml = -10
  phi <- plogis(as.vector(Xhi %*% b2))                  # n predictions at deml = +10

  dd_est[i] <- mean(phi - plo)                          # average the n differences

  g <- colMeans(phi * (1 - phi) * Xhi) - colMeans(plo * (1 - plo) * Xlo)
  dd_sd[i] <- sqrt(as.numeric(t(g) %*% V2 %*% g))
}

me_d <- tibble(lncaprat = cr_grid, est = ame_est, se = ame_se,
               panel = "A. Derivative: per one-point move")
me_c <- tibble(lncaprat = cr_grid, est = dd_est,  se = dd_sd,
               panel = "B. Discrete: full -10 to +10 move")

me_panel <- function(d) d %>%
  mutate(lo = est - 1.96 * se, hi = est + 1.96 * se) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = lncaprat, y = est)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = bu_palegreen, alpha = 0.45) +
  geom_line(color = bu_green, linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = bu_grey) +
  geom_rug(data = slice_sample(dp, n = 1500), aes(x = lncaprat), inherit.aes = FALSE,
           alpha = 0.15, color = bu_grey) +
  labs(title = unique(d$panel), x = "ln(capability ratio)", y = "change in Pr(dispute)") +
  theme_bu() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 11, face = "bold"),
        panel.border = element_rect(color = bu_grey, fill = NA, linewidth = 0.3))

me_panel(me_d) | me_panel(me_c)








Figure 10: Two marginal effects of democracy from the same model. Left: the average derivative, the change in Pr(dispute) per one-point move in democracy. Right: the average discrete change over the full range of democracy. Both at each value of the capability ratio, with delta-method intervals.





In either panel, the finding is that becoming more democratic reduces the chances of conflict for dyads at parity, but has little or no effect for dyads with imbalances. Put differently, the marginal effect of an increase in democracy is to decrease the chances of conflict across the range of capabilities, but that dampening effect gets smaller as capability ratios get larger. By the time ln(capabilities) reaches about 5, democracy exerts no measurable effect on conflict.
Panel B is a better one for these data - it’s differenced and set up between the cases where Polity is -10 and +10. We can say something explicit about the change in \(x\) here, and the effects are on a more meaningful scale because of the large change in \(x\). The marginal effect of moving from -10 to +10 on Polity for a dyad at parity is to reduce the chances of conflict by about 8 percentage points. Again, because Polity is discrete, this is a marginally more appropriate method, though you can see in the figures it really doesn’t matter.
Compare these to the predicted probabilities and you’ll see they tell the same basic story. In Figure 9, reading left-to-right, you can see the probability of conflict for a dyad at parity declines over the range of democracy from about 9.5% to something close to zero. In Figure 10, reading just at the left side, for dyads at parity, an increase in democracy is associated with a decrease of about 8 percentage points in the chance of conflict. These are just different ways to represent and discuss conditional effects.

Answer key for Exercise #5. Part I is the construction and the checks against it; Part II is the polynomial comparison, which has a genuinely interesting answer; Part III is the hazard and the survivor function with simulated intervals, built step by step, and the same quantities with delta-method intervals alongside.
The regime measure here is Polity V. A V-Dem index is an equally good answer and will produce a slightly different estimation sample.

title: Exercise #5 — Build the Spell Data, Then Model the Hazard (Answers)
text:
1. The construction

archigos <- read_dta("https://www.rochester.edu/college/faculty/hgoemans/Archigos_4.1_stata14.dta") %>%
  mutate(startdate = as.Date(startdate),
         enddate   = as.Date(enddate),
         startyr   = as.numeric(format(startdate, "%Y")),
         endyr     = as.numeric(format(enddate,   "%Y")),
         spellyrs  = (endyr - startyr) + 1)            # calendar years the spell touches

# check spellyrs: the longest spell, and no zero or negative lengths
range(archigos$spellyrs)

[1]  1 69

# expand: each spell's row repeated spellyrs times
leaderyears <- uncount(archigos, spellyrs)

# check: still 3,409 spells
n_distinct(leaderyears$obsid)

[1] 3409

# year: the spell's first calendar year, then one more for each row after it
leaderyears <- leaderyears %>%
  group_by(obsid) %>%                                  # obsid = the SPELL, not the person
  mutate(year = startyr - 1 + row_number()) %>%
  ungroup()

# survival time, censoring, and failure
leaderyears <- leaderyears %>%
  arrange(obsid, year) %>%
  group_by(obsid) %>%
  mutate(t          = row_number(),                    # years in office so far
         censor     = if_else(exit == "Still in Office" & t == n(), 1, 0),
         leftoffice = if_else(censor == 0 & t == n(), 1, 0)) %>%
  ungroup()

These lines of code correspond to the three decisions:
spellyrs = (endyr - startyr) + 1, counted on calendar years, is the partial-year decision: a spell running November to February occupies two rows. The alternative — counting only whole years in office — is defensible, but would produce a different file. What is not defensible is failing to notice and make an explicit choice.
group_by(obsid) is the spell decision. leadid identifies the person, and 457 people held office more than once. Grouping by the person runs their separate spells together and counts the years they were out of power as time survived.
exit == "Still in Office", in the censor line, is the censoring decision. Without it, every spell’s last row is a failure and the 165 leaders in power on 31 December 2015 and 3 still in power at the end of 2014 are recorded as having left. They had not; we stopped watching.
