6. Comparing fit
Two tools, doing two different jobs. These models are nested — each adds one term to the last — so a likelihood-ratio test applies: \(-2(\ln L_{\text{restricted}} - \ln L_{\text{full}})\), distributed \(\chi^2\) with degrees of freedom equal to the number of added parameters.

lr <- function(a, b, lab) {
  x <- anova(a, b, test = "LRT")
  tibble(comparison = lab, LR = round(x$Deviance[2], 2), df = x$Df[2],
         p = format.pval(x$`Pr(>Chi)`[2], digits = 3))
}
bind_rows(lr(m0, m1, "no time -> t"),
          lr(m1, m2, "t -> t, t²"),
          lr(m2, m3, "t, t² -> t, t², t³")) %>%

What each is doing. The likelihood-ratio test asks a hypothesis question: is the added coefficient different from zero? With \(n = 16{,}068\) it will answer yes to very small improvements, because it does not penalize parameters at all. The information criteria ask a different question — which model would predict best out of sample? — and they penalize for additinoal parameters: AIC charges 2 per parameter, BIC charges \(\log(16{,}068) = 9.68\).
Do they agree? Mostly, and where they part is the interesting bit. Every LR step is significant, including the cubic (\(\chi^2 = 9.95\), \(p = 0.0016\)). AIC picks the cubic outright, 14630.1 against 14638.0. BIC cannot separate the quadratic from the cubic: 14730.2 against 14730.0, a gap of 0.26 — nothing at all on any of the usual scales. BIC’s stiffer penalty eats almost the whole gain from the third term.

title: Exercise #5 — Build the Spell Data, Then Model the Hazard (Answers)
text:
7. Which model to keep
Both answers are defensible.
For the cubic: the LR test and AIC both endorse it, the \(t^3\) coefficient is individually significant, and the cost of one extra parameter on 16,068 observations is trivial. If the baseline hazard’s shape is the object of interest — and in a hazard model it usually is — you want the flexibility.
For the quadratic: BIC says the third term buys 0.2, which is nothing, and a term that survives only the most permissive of three criteria is a thin reed. The quadratic already permits a non-monotonic baseline, which is the substantive requirement.
What I do not want is “the cubic, because \(p < 0.05\).” Significance on 16,000 observations is cheap, and the whole point of putting AIC and BIC next to the LR test is to see them disagree and have to choose. I use the cubic from here on, though the quadratic would give visually indistinguishable figures — which is itself the strongest argument that the choice does not much matter. I prefer the cubic because it is more general in the sense that it relaxes the one-inflection point assumption.

8. Leader age across the four models

tibble(model = c("no time", "t", "t, t²", "t, t², t³"),
       age = map_dbl(list(m0, m1, m2, m3), ~ coef(.x)["age"]),
       polity = map_dbl(list(m0, m1, m2, m3), ~ coef(.x)["polity2"])) %>%
  mutate(across(age:polity, ~ round(.x, 4))) %>%

The age coefficient climbs from 0.0159 to 0.0221, about 38%, and the answer is that it is not about age. Leaders age while they hold office: survival time and leader age are mechanically correlated. In a model with no measure of survival, age is the only variable available to absorb duration dependence, and it does so quietly, and with the wrong label on it insofar as we think of it as age, but it’s also measuring survival. Adding the survival baseline allows age to measure its independent effect explicitly.
Polity moves the other way, 0.054 to 0.039, for the same reason in reverse: some of what looked like a democracy effect was the composition of long and short spells.
The general lesson: whenever a covariate is mechanically related to time in the spell, leaving the baseline hazard unmodeled loads that covariate with work it should not be doing. This is a very specific kind of omitted-variable bias.

title: Exercise #5 — Build the Spell Data, Then Model the Hazard (Answers)
text:
The build

Step 1 — The three pieces
A predicted probability needs the coefficients and a row of data. An interval around it needs the covariance matrix as well.

b <- coef(m3)                     # k coefficients, a named vector
V <- vcov(m3)                     # k x k covariance matrix
k <- length(b)
n <- nobs(m3)

c(cases = n, coefficients = k)

       cases coefficients 
       16068           13 




Step 2 — The counterfactual design matrix
“Average effects” means: change the variable of interest for every case, leave each case’s own age, gender, route to power and region alone, predict, and average. So the first step is a copy of the data with the variables of interest overwritten. est_cf5 is the estimation sample, counterfactual version: every row of est, with polity2 and the spell clock overwritten and every other column left exactly as that leader-year had it. Same rows, same \(n\). The clock is three columns — t, t2, and t3 — and all three have to change together.
model.matrix() then turns that data frame into the numeric matrix glm actually used: factors become dummy columns, one per non-reference category.

est_cf5 <- est %>% mutate(polity2 = 0, t = 5, t2 = 5^2, t3 = 5^3)   # Polity 0, year 5

# formula(m3)[-2] drops the left-hand side, because no outcome variable is needed
X5 <- model.matrix(formula(m3)[-2], data = est_cf5)

dim(X5)                           # n rows, k columns

[1] 16068    13



Step 2a — Reading the square brackets
X5 has two dimensions, so it takes two indices separated by a comma. Leaving a slot empty means “all of them”:








X5[j, 4]
row \(j\), column 4
one number


X5[j, ]
row \(j\), every column
a vector of length \(k\) — one case


X5[, 4]
every row, column 4
a vector of length \(n\) — one variable



The comma is what tells R the object is two-dimensional. Without it, R treats the matrix as one long vector running down the columns, which is legal and almost never what you meant.

length(X5[1, ])            # k -- one case, all its variables

[1] 13

length(X5[, 1])            # n -- one variable, all the cases

[1] 16068

X5[2]                      # no comma: element 2 counting down column 1 -- not row 2

[1] 1

X5[2, 1]                   # the same element, with both indices written out

[1] 1

is.matrix(X5[1, ])         # a single row comes back as a plain vector

[1] FALSE


X5[j, ] comes back as a plain vector, not a one-row matrix. That is why sum(X5[j, ] * b) works below, and why t(g) %*% V %*% g works for the standard error.



Step 3 — One case
Let’s choose one row - Margaret Thatcher’s fifth year in office is 1983; the UK’s actual Polity score that year is 10, and est_cf5 has set it to 0.

i <- which(est$leader == "Thatcher" & est$t == 5)

est[i, c("leader", "idacr", "year", "t", "age", "female", "entry", "region", "polity2")]

# A tibble: 1 × 9
  leader   idacr  year     t   age female entry   region polity2
  <chr>    <chr> <dbl> <int> <dbl>  <int> <fct>   <fct>    <dbl>
1 Thatcher UKG    1983     5    58      1 Regular Europe      10

# her row of the design matrix, term by term
tibble(term = colnames(X5), x = X5[i, ], b = b, contribution = X5[i, ] * b)

# A tibble: 13 × 4
   term                        x          b contribution
   <chr>                   <dbl>      <dbl>        <dbl>
 1 (Intercept)                 1 -2.35          -2.35   
 2 t                           5 -0.0300        -0.150  
 3 t2                         25 -0.00221       -0.0552 
 4 t3                        125  0.0000589      0.00736
 5 polity2                     0  0.0389         0      
 6 age                        58  0.0221         1.28   
 7 female                      1 -0.326         -0.326  
 8 entryIrregular              0  0.411          0      
 9 entryForeign Imposition     0  0.0677         0      
10 regionAmericas              0 -0.125          0      
11 regionAfrica                0 -0.760          0      
12 regionMiddle East           0 -0.572          0      
13 regionAsia/Oceania          0 -0.327          0      


Two things to see in her row: female is 1, and all four region dummies are 0, because Europe is the reference category — there is no regionEurope column for it to occupy. The linear predictor is the last column added up, and the hazard is the logistic function of it.

eta_i <- sum(X5[i, ] * b)                    # x_i'b -- one number
h_i   <- 1 / (1 + exp(-eta_i))               # same as plogis(eta_i)

c(eta = eta_i, h = h_i)

       eta          h 
-1.5961082  0.1685262 


The gradient is what the delta-method interval will need later: how \(h_i\) moves when each coefficient moves. For the logit, \(\partial h / \partial \eta = h(1-h)\), so by the chain rule the derivative with respect to coefficient \(m\) is \(h(1-h)\) times that case’s \(x_m\).

w_i <- h_i * (1 - h_i)                       # one number
g_i <- w_i * X5[i, ]                         # k numbers, one per coefficient

round(g_i, 5)

            (Intercept)                       t                      t2 
                0.14013                 0.70063                 3.50313 
                     t3                 polity2                     age 
               17.51564                 0.00000                 8.12726 
                 female          entryIrregular entryForeign Imposition 
                0.14013                 0.00000                 0.00000 
         regionAmericas            regionAfrica       regionMiddle East 
                0.00000                 0.00000                 0.00000 
     regionAsia/Oceania 
                0.00000 




Step 4 — Three cases: what “average” is an average of
Three leader-years, all set to Polity 0 and year 5, differing only in the covariates they brought with them.

three <- c(which(est$leader == "Thatcher" & est$t == 5),
           which(est$leader == "Mandela"  & est$t == 5),
           which(est$leader == "Nyerere"  & est$t == 5))

h_three <- numeric(3)
for (r in 1:3) {
  h_three[r] <- 1 / (1 + exp(-sum(X5[three[r], ] * b)))
}

tibble(leader = est$leader[three], year = est$year[three], age = est$age[three],
       region = est$region[three], h = round(h_three, 4))

# A tibble: 3 × 5
  leader    year   age region      h
  <chr>    <dbl> <dbl> <fct>   <dbl>
1 Thatcher  1983    58 Europe 0.168 
2 Mandela   1998    80 Africa 0.176 
3 Nyerere   1965    43 Africa 0.0862

mean(h_three)              # the average hazard over these three cases

[1] 0.1435196


The next step does exactly this over all 16,068 rows instead of three.


Step 5 — All cases: the average hazard and its gradient
One pass over the rows, accumulating two running totals: the hazards, and the gradients. Dividing each by \(n\) at the end gives the average and its gradient.

h_sum <- 0
g_sum <- rep(0, k)

for (j in 1:n) {
  eta_j <- sum(X5[j, ] * b)
  h_j   <- 1 / (1 + exp(-eta_j))
  w_j   <- h_j * (1 - h_j)

  h_sum <- h_sum + h_j
  g_sum <- g_sum + w_j * X5[j, ]              # add this case's k-vector to the total
}

hbar_loop <- h_sum / n
g_loop    <- g_sum / n

Here are the same two quantities without the loop. X5 %*% b does all \(n\) linear predictors at once, and colMeans averages down the columns — that is, over cases.

pr       <- plogis(as.vector(X5 %*% b))       # n hazards
hbar_vec <- mean(pr)
g_vec    <- colMeans((pr * (1 - pr)) * X5)    # each row scaled by its own w, then averaged

c(loop = hbar_loop, vectorized = hbar_vec)

      loop vectorized 
 0.1833263  0.1833263 

all.equal(g_loop, g_vec)

[1] TRUE


Compare that to the three-case average: three cases average to 0.144, all 16,068 average to 0.183. The estimand is the second one.
The averaging runs over cases, at fixed coefficients. Averaging the \(k\) columns instead would collapse the gradient to one number. Averaging over coefficient draws is a third thing, and that one is the simulation in Step 11.


Step 6 — The standard error of that average
The delta method keeps the coefficients at b and uses calculus for the uncertainty: \(\text{se} = \sqrt{g'\mathbf{V}g}\), with \(g\) the gradient built in Step 5. Written out, that is a sum over every pair of coefficients — each pair’s covariance, weighted by both their gradients. With \(k = 13\) there are 169 pairs.

var_loop <- 0
for (r in 1:k) {
  for (cc in 1:k) {
    var_loop <- var_loop + g_loop[r] * V[r, cc] * g_loop[cc]
  }
}

var_matrix <- as.numeric(t(g_vec) %*% V %*% g_vec)     # the same 169 products

c(loop = sqrt(var_loop), matrix = sqrt(var_matrix))

loop.(Intercept)           matrix 
     0.004200381      0.004200381 

# the interval, on the probability scale
hbar_vec + c(-1.96, 0, 1.96) * sqrt(var_matrix)

[1] 0.1750935 0.1833263 0.1915590




Step 7 — Every year of tenure
Steps 2 through 6 did one year. Now do 25 of them, so the results need somewhere to live: two vectors of length 25, and a matrix with one row per year and one column per coefficient — because each year has a whole gradient, not a number.

tmax <- 25                 # years of tenure to plot

hbar <- numeric(tmax)
se_h <- numeric(tmax)
G    <- matrix(NA, tmax, k)
colnames(G) <- names(b)

for (i in 1:tmax) {
  est_cf <- est %>% mutate(polity2 = 0, t = i, t2 = i^2, t3 = i^3)
  Xi <- model.matrix(formula(m3)[-2], data = est_cf)

  pr      <- plogis(as.vector(Xi %*% b))
  hbar[i] <- mean(pr)
  G[i, ]  <- colMeans((pr * (1 - pr)) * Xi)                  # write a k-vector into row i
  se_h[i] <- sqrt(as.numeric(t(G[i, ]) %*% V %*% G[i, ]))    # read row i back out
}

dim(G)                     # 25 x k

[1] 25 13

length(G[3, ])             # k -- year 3's gradient, all coefficients

[1] 13

length(G[, 3])             # 25 -- coefficient 3's gradient, all years

[1] 25

head(tibble(t = 1:tmax, h = hbar, se = se_h,
            lo = hbar - 1.96 * se_h, hi = hbar + 1.96 * se_h))

# A tibble: 6 × 5
      t     h      se    lo    hi
  <int> <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1     1 0.209 0.00587 0.197 0.220
2     2 0.203 0.00460 0.194 0.212
3     3 0.197 0.00401 0.189 0.205
4     4 0.190 0.00396 0.182 0.198
5     5 0.183 0.00420 0.175 0.192
6     6 0.176 0.00451 0.167 0.185




Step 8 — The survivor function: a running product and a running sum
Surviving to \(t\) means not failing in year 1, and not failing in year 2, and so on. Each of those is a conditional probability, so they multiply:
\[S(t) = \prod_{j \le t}\left\{1 - \bar h(j)\right\}\]
\(1 - \bar h(j)\) is the chance of getting through year \(j\) having reached it, and the running product is the chance of getting through all of them. The \(\bar h(j)\) are the average hazards from Step 7 — nothing new is estimated here.
The delta method needs the gradient of that product. Every \(\bar h(j)\) in it is a function of the same \(\beta\), so the gradient adds one term per year, with \(g(j)\) the gradient of \(\bar h(j)\) from Step 7:
\[
\frac{\partial S(t)}{\partial \beta} = -S(t) \sum_{j \leq t} \frac{g(j)}{1 - \bar h(j)}
\]
The two accumulators below run side by side — one multiplying, one adding — on the Polity 0 hazards and gradients from Step 7.

S    <- numeric(tmax)
se_S <- numeric(tmax)

running_S <- 1                       # the product so far
running_q <- rep(0, k)               # the summed gradient so far, a k-vector

for (i in 1:tmax) {
  running_S <- running_S * (1 - hbar[i])
  running_q <- running_q + G[i, ] / (1 - hbar[i])

  S[i]    <- running_S
  se_S[i] <- running_S * sqrt(as.numeric(t(running_q) %*% V %*% running_q))
}

cumprod and cumsum are those two accumulators, written compactly.

S_vec    <- cumprod(1 - hbar)
Q        <- apply(G / (1 - hbar), 2, cumsum)      # 25 x k: row i is running_q at year i
se_S_vec <- S_vec * sqrt(rowSums((Q %*% V) * Q))  # sqrt(q'Vq) for all 25 rows at once

c(all.equal(S, S_vec), all.equal(se_S, se_S_vec))

[1] TRUE TRUE


What the running sum is for: here is the same calculation with the 25 years treated as independent of each other, which is what dropping it amounts to. At \(t = 1\) the two agree, because there is only one term to accumulate.

se_S_wrong <- numeric(tmax)
for (i in 1:tmax) {
  se_S_wrong[i] <- sqrt(sum((S[i] / (1 - hbar[1:i]))^2 * se_h[1:i]^2))
}

tibble(t = 1:tmax, S = round(S, 3),
       se_correct = round(se_S, 4), se_independent = round(se_S_wrong, 4)) %>%
  filter(t %in% c(1, 5, 10, 25))

# A tibble: 4 × 4
      t     S se_correct se_independent
  <int> <dbl>      <dbl>          <dbl>
1     1 0.791     0.0059         0.0059
2     5 0.335     0.0083         0.0043
3    10 0.138     0.0062         0.0025
4    25 0.027     0.0029         0.0008




Step 9 — The full grid: the delta method end to end
This step stands on its own. Every setting it uses is re-declared here, and Steps 2 through 8 are its body: build the counterfactual design matrix, average the predictions over cases, average the gradients, accumulate the product for \(S(t)\). Nothing new happens below — it is the same work inside one more loop.

b     <- coef(m3)                  # k coefficients
V     <- vcov(m3)                  # k x k covariance matrix
k     <- length(b)
tmax  <- 25                        # years of tenure to plot
pvals <- c(-10, 0, 10)             # the three counterfactual Polity values

qi <- tibble()                     # results pile up here, one block per Polity value

for (p in pvals) {

  # the hazard at each year: Steps 2, 5, 6 and 7, inside one loop
  hbar <- numeric(tmax)            # average hazard, one per year
  se_h <- numeric(tmax)            # its standard error
  G    <- matrix(NA, tmax, k)      # its gradient: one ROW per year, one column per coefficient

  for (i in 1:tmax) {
    est_cf <- est %>% mutate(polity2 = p, t = i, t2 = i^2, t3 = i^3)   # the counterfactual
    Xi <- model.matrix(formula(m3)[-2], data = est_cf)                 # n x k

    pr      <- plogis(as.vector(Xi %*% b))        # n predicted hazards
    hbar[i] <- mean(pr)                           # averaged over CASES
    G[i, ]  <- colMeans((pr * (1 - pr)) * Xi)     # each row scaled by its own w, then averaged
    se_h[i] <- sqrt(as.numeric(t(G[i, ]) %*% V %*% G[i, ]))        # sqrt(g'Vg)
  }

  # the survivor function: Step 8
  S    <- numeric(tmax)
  se_S <- numeric(tmax)

  running_S <- 1                   # the product so far
  running_q <- rep(0, k)           # the summed gradient so far

  for (i in 1:tmax) {
    running_S <- running_S * (1 - hbar[i])
    running_q <- running_q + G[i, ] / (1 - hbar[i])

    S[i]    <- running_S
    se_S[i] <- running_S * sqrt(as.numeric(t(running_q) %*% V %*% running_q))
  }

  qi <- bind_rows(qi, tibble(polity = p, t = 1:tmax,
                             h = hbar, h_se = se_h, s = S, s_se = se_S))
}

qi <- qi %>%
  mutate(h_lo = h - 1.96 * h_se, h_hi = h + 1.96 * h_se,
         s_lo = s - 1.96 * s_se, s_hi = s + 1.96 * s_se,
         polity = factor(polity, levels = pvals,
                         labels = c("Polity -10", "Polity 0", "Polity +10")))

qi

# A tibble: 75 × 10
   polity         t     h    h_se     s    s_se   h_lo  h_hi  s_lo  s_hi
   <fct>      <int> <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
 1 Polity -10     1 0.153 0.00790 0.847 0.00790 0.137  0.168 0.832 0.863
 2 Polity -10     2 0.148 0.00715 0.722 0.0127  0.134  0.162 0.697 0.746
 3 Polity -10     3 0.143 0.00669 0.618 0.0156  0.130  0.157 0.588 0.649
 4 Polity -10     4 0.138 0.00643 0.533 0.0172  0.126  0.151 0.499 0.566
 5 Polity -10     5 0.133 0.00626 0.462 0.0180  0.121  0.145 0.427 0.497
 6 Polity -10     6 0.127 0.00614 0.403 0.0183  0.115  0.139 0.367 0.439
 7 Polity -10     7 0.122 0.00601 0.354 0.0182  0.110  0.134 0.318 0.390
 8 Polity -10     8 0.116 0.00586 0.313 0.0179  0.105  0.128 0.278 0.348

10 Polity -10    10 0.106 0.00548 0.249 0.0170  0.0949 0.116 0.215 0.282
# ℹ 65 more rows




Step 10 — The two figures

ggplot(qi, aes(t, h, color = polity, fill = polity, linetype = polity)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = h_lo, ymax = h_hi), alpha = 0.45, color = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(bu_black, bu_lightgreen, bu_green)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(bu_black, bu_lightgreen, bu_green)) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = bu_lty[1:3]) +
  labs(title = "Annual hazard of leaving office",
       subtitle = "every leader-year set to each Polity value; 95% delta-method intervals",
       x = "Years in office", y = "h(t)",
       color = NULL, fill = NULL, linetype = NULL) +   # linetype = NULL, or ggplot draws two legends
  theme_bu() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")







Figure 1






ggplot(qi, aes(t, s, color = polity, fill = polity, linetype = polity)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = s_lo, ymax = s_hi), alpha = 0.45, color = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, color = bu_grey, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(bu_black, bu_lightgreen, bu_green)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(bu_black, bu_lightgreen, bu_green)) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = bu_lty[1:3]) +
  labs(title = "Share of leaders still in office",
       subtitle = "same model and same counterfactuals as the hazard figure",
       x = "Years in office", y = "S(t)",
       color = NULL, fill = NULL, linetype = NULL) +
  theme_bu() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")







Figure 2







Step 11 — The same quantities by simulation
This step stands on its own too. Every setting it uses is re-declared, so it can be read, or run, without Steps 2 through 10 in front of you.

b      <- coef(m3)                 # k coefficients
V      <- vcov(m3)                 # k x k covariance matrix
k      <- length(b)
tmax   <- 25                       # years of tenure to plot
pvals  <- c(-10, 0, 10)            # the three counterfactual Polity values
ndraws <- 1000                     # coefficient vectors to draw

# the counterfactual design matrix at Polity 0 and year 5, rebuilt: every case
# as it would look under that counterfactual, its own covariates untouched
est_cf5_sim <- est %>% mutate(polity2 = 0, t = 5, t2 = 5^2, t3 = 5^3)
X5_sim      <- model.matrix(formula(m3)[-2], data = est_cf5_sim)

dim(X5_sim)                        # n cases x k coefficients

[1] 16068    13



Step 11a — What a draw is
Steps 2 through 10 held the coefficients fixed at b and used calculus for the uncertainty. Simulation holds nothing fixed: it draws 1,000 plausible coefficient vectors from the model’s own sampling distribution, \(N(\widehat\beta, \mathbf{V})\), and recomputes the whole quantity once per draw. One draw is one row of sims — a complete alternative set of coefficients, near b and correlated the way V says they are.

set.seed(20260916)   # fix the seed right before the draws, so anything run or printed
                     # earlier cannot shift them
sims <- MASS::mvrnorm(ndraws, b, V)      # ndraws rows, one draw each; k columns

dim(sims)

[1] 1000   13

b_draw1 <- sims[1, ]
round(cbind(estimate = b, draw1 = b_draw1), 4)

                        estimate   draw1
(Intercept)              -2.3516 -2.1597
t                        -0.0300 -0.0401
t2                       -0.0022 -0.0018
t3                        0.0001  0.0001
polity2                   0.0389  0.0350
age                       0.0221  0.0212
female                   -0.3257 -0.3817
entryIrregular            0.4109  0.3579
entryForeign Imposition   0.0677  0.0688
regionAmericas           -0.1253 -0.2161
regionAfrica             -0.7596 -0.7438
regionMiddle East        -0.5722 -0.6439
regionAsia/Oceania       -0.3270 -0.3036


That draw’s average hazard is the Step 5 calculation with b_draw1 in place of b: \(n\) predictions, averaged over cases.

mean(plogis(as.vector(X5_sim %*% b_draw1)))

[1] 0.1933044




Step 11b — All the draws at one year
Now every draw, still at Polity 0 and year 5. Each pass of the loop produces one number: an average over the \(n\) cases, at that draw’s coefficients.

h_draws_loop <- numeric(ndraws)
for (d in 1:ndraws) {
  h_draws_loop[d] <- mean(plogis(as.vector(X5_sim %*% sims[d, ])))
}

The compact form of that loop. X5_sim %*% t(sims) is an \(n \times 1000\) matrix — one row per case, one column per draw — so each column holds \(x_i\beta\) for every case under one draw’s coefficients. plogis() turns that into predicted probabilities, and colMeans averages down each column, over cases: one average prediction per draw.

h_draws_vec <- colMeans(plogis(X5_sim %*% t(sims)))    # ndraws average hazards

all.equal(h_draws_loop, h_draws_vec)

[1] TRUE


rowMeans on that same matrix averages the other way, over draws within a case: \(n\) numbers describing different leaders, not 1,000 describing estimation uncertainty. Both calls run; only one answers the question.

length(colMeans(plogis(X5_sim %*% t(sims))))     # ndraws -- the sampling distribution

[1] 1000

length(rowMeans(plogis(X5_sim %*% t(sims))))     # n      -- one number per leader-year

[1] 16068


The interval is the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of those 1,000 values.

quantile(h_draws_vec, c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975))

     2.5%       50%     97.5% 
0.1751696 0.1833743 0.1916925 




Step 11c — The full grid
Every year of tenure from 1 to 25, at three values of Polity. Nothing new happens — it is the same work inside two more loops. For each Polity value, hmat holds years down the rows and draws across the columns. \(S(t)\) is built within a draw — cumprod down one column at a time — so each draw’s survivor curve uses that draw’s own 25 hazards.
The interval at each year comes from the 1,000 values in that row. apply(X, MARGIN, FUN) runs a function over one dimension of a matrix: X is the matrix, MARGIN is the dimension (1 for rows, 2 for columns), and FUN is the function run along it — here the median and the two percentiles. colMeans(M) is the same thing as apply(M, 2, mean).

M <- matrix(1:6, nrow = 2)     # 2 x 3

apply(M, 1, sum)     # 9 12      -- 2 values, one per ROW    (rows kept)

[1]  9 12

apply(M, 2, sum)     # 3 7 11    -- 3 values, one per COLUMN (columns kept)

[1]  3  7 11


Each draw also has its own median tenure — the first year its \(S(t)\) drops below .5 — so median tenure gets an interval the same way: the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of 1,000 of them.

first_below <- function(x) {             # the first year a survivor curve is below .5
  w <- which(x < 0.5)
  if (length(w)) w[1] else NA_integer_
}

sim_qi <- tibble()
tenure <- tibble()

for (p in pvals) {

  hmat <- matrix(NA, tmax, ndraws)         # years down the rows, draws across

  for (i in 1:tmax) {
    est_cf <- est %>% mutate(polity2 = p, t = i, t2 = i^2, t3 = i^3)
    Xi <- model.matrix(formula(m3)[-2], data = est_cf)
    hmat[i, ] <- colMeans(plogis(Xi %*% t(sims)))   # row i: this year, every draw
  }

  smat <- matrix(NA, tmax, ndraws)
  for (d in 1:ndraws) {
    smat[, d] <- cumprod(1 - hmat[, d])    # this draw's 25 hazards, chained
  }

  # intervals across the draws at each year: apply over ROWS
  sim_qi <- bind_rows(sim_qi,
    tibble(polity = p, t = 1:tmax,
           sim_h    = apply(hmat, 1, median),
           sim_h_lo = apply(hmat, 1, quantile, 0.025),
           sim_h_hi = apply(hmat, 1, quantile, 0.975),
           sim_s    = apply(smat, 1, median),
           sim_s_lo = apply(smat, 1, quantile, 0.025),
           sim_s_hi = apply(smat, 1, quantile, 0.975)))

  # one median tenure per draw: apply over COLUMNS
  med <- apply(smat, 2, first_below)
  tenure <- bind_rows(tenure, tibble(
    Polity                     = p,
    `Median tenure (yrs)`      = quantile(med, 0.5, type = 1, names = FALSE),
    `95% interval`             = sprintf("[%.0f, %.0f]", quantile(med, 0.025, type = 1),
                                                         quantile(med, 0.975, type = 1)),
    `Still in office at 5 yrs` = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * median(smat[5, ])),
    `at 10 yrs`                = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * median(smat[10, ]))))
}

sim_plot <- sim_qi %>%
  mutate(polity = factor(polity, levels = pvals,
                         labels = c("Polity -10", "Polity 0", "Polity +10")))

Same model, same counterfactuals as Step 10; the only difference is where the interval came from — percentiles of 1,000 draws here, \(\sqrt{g'\mathbf{V}g}\) there. Side by side at Polity 0:

left_join(sim_plot, qi, by = c("polity", "t")) %>%
  filter(polity == "Polity 0", t %in% c(1, 5, 10, 25)) %>%
  dplyr::select(t, sim_h, sim_h_lo, sim_h_hi, h, h_lo, h_hi) %>%
  mutate(across(-t, ~ round(.x, 3))) %>%
  kbl(caption = "The hazard at Polity 0: simulated (sim_) and delta-method intervals.") %>%
  kable_styling("striped", full_width = FALSE, font_size = 16)

title: Exercise #5 — Build the Spell Data, Then Model the Hazard (Answers)
text:
9. The hazard across survival time
The answer uses the simulated quantities from Step 11.

ggplot(sim_plot, aes(t, sim_h, color = polity, fill = polity, linetype = polity)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = sim_h_lo, ymax = sim_h_hi), alpha = 0.45, color = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(bu_black, bu_lightgreen, bu_green)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(bu_black, bu_lightgreen, bu_green)) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = bu_lty[1:3]) +
  labs(title = "Annual hazard of leaving office",
       subtitle = "95% simulated intervals: 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of 1,000 draws",
       x = "Years in office", y = "h(t)",
       color = NULL, fill = NULL, linetype = NULL) +
  theme_bu() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")







Figure 3





Read as an article would: the annual risk of losing office is higher in democracies at every point in a leader’s tenure — 0.28 against 0.15 in the first year — and it declines slowly in both, so a leader who has already survived a decade faces a lower risk than a newcomer but nothing like safety.
The bands are worth a comment. They separate cleanly out to about twenty years and begin to overlap after that — the first adjacent overlap is at \(t = 24\). That is not a failure of the model; it is the estimation sample thinning out. Very few leaders survive two decades, so there is little information about the hazard there, and the intervals say so.
